articles.title: Iraqi factions propose weapons 'freeze' instead of disarmament
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Exclusive: Iraqi factions propose weapons 'freeze' instead of disarmament
Iraqi armed factions have proposed placing their weapons in their own storage facilities and suspending military activity for two years, rather than handing their arsenals to the state, political sources close to the governing Coordination Framework told The New Arab.
The proposal, which Baghdad has rejected, highlights the obstacles facing Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s government as it seeks to bring all weapons under state control without triggering a confrontation with Iran-aligned groups in the country.
Three Iraqi political sources, including a senior parliamentarian, said the government received the proposal in recent days. Under the plan, unnamed factions would halt armed operations and place their weapons in designated warehouses for two years, but would retain control of them rather than transfer them to Iraqi security forces.
A senior Iraqi MP told The New Arab that Kataib Hezbollah was among the groups to have proposed freezing its weapons in private depots and ceasing armed activity inside Iraq for two years.
The group also linked the proposal to the future of US forces in Iraq and demanded assurances that its leaders would not be targeted, the MP said, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter.
"The government rejected the proposal, considering it an attempt to circumvent the principle of ending weapons outside the official security forces," the lawmaker said.
Baghdad is using intermediaries including former Council fo Representatives member Hadi al-Ameri, National Security Adviser Qasim al-Araji and Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) chief Faleh al-Fayyadh to engage with the armed groups, according to the source. No direct meeting has yet taken place between Zaidi and faction leaders or their representatives.
Resistance to disarmament
The most influential factions, with close ties to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, continue to reject surrendering their weapons, while warning they could escalate against the government if it attempts to use force.
Kataib Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba, Kataib al-Wafiyoun and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada have in recent weeks issued public statements setting conditions for any discussion of their weapons.
These include the withdrawal of US and Turkish forces from Iraq, the dismantling of the Kurdistan Region’s Peshmerga forces, an end to what they describe as US influence over Iraq’s political, economic and financial decision-making, and the expulsion of US companies.
Other groups, including Badr, Kataib al-Tufuf and Harakat al-Abdal, have not publicly set out their positions.
Zaidi said last week that his government did not intend to clash militarily with the factions, describing the effort to monopolise weapons in state hands as a "constructive dialogue".
He said some groups had handed over weapons, severed their organisational ties and joined the state-sanctioned PMF, while talks continued with others. Zaidi said political forces broadly supported the effort, which he described as consistent with Iraq’s constitution and necessary to strengthen state authority and stability.
However, sources close to the Coordination Framework said proposals to regulate or freeze the weapons, rather than surrender them, had found little support within the government. They said such arrangements were also unlikely to satisfy Washington or neighbouring states concerned about factions’ drones and missiles, including weapons with a range exceeding 100 kilometres.
Limited visibility over arsenals
A former Iraqi government adviser told The New Arab that Baghdad does not have a reliable database detailing the quantity or types of weapons held by the factions — a gap that makes official claims of progress difficult to assess.
He said the consensus in Baghdad was to avoid a military confrontation, including raids on faction bases and camps, because of the risk of a wider internal conflict and Iran’s influence over the groups.
The Iraqi state has received weapons from several factions, including Harakat al-Imam Ali and Asaib Ahl al-Haq, he said. But the equipment handed over was limited and did not reflect the groups’ full capabilities.
The adviser said Kataib Hezbollah, Harakat al-Nujaba and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada remained the three main factions unwilling even to make a symbolic handover. Together, the groups have around 30,000 fighters affiliated with the PMF, he said, although their organisational structures and armaments remain tied to their respective factions.
Pressure from Washington
Iraqi political researcher Ali al-Taie warned that continued failure to make progress could prompt Washington to withdraw support for Zaidi’s government and revive the use of sanctions against Iraqi state and private-sector bodies.
He argued that Washington would view any formula short of the surrender of drones and missiles as an attempt to evade disarmament. The US, he added, is unlikely to accept transfer of weapons to the PMF as a sufficient solution, viewing many of the factions and the umbrella force as closely intertwined.
Kataib Hezbollah renewed its rejection of disarmament in a statement on 18 August, issuing threats against Zaidi and accusing him of pursuing US-backed policies. The group said that any arrangement with the government required the withdrawal of US forces, the removal of Turkish troops from northern Iraq and the dismantling of the Peshmerga.
Earlier this month, Iraqi MP and parliamentary security committee member Othman al-Shaybani said Zaidi had warned that failure to resolve the weapons issue could invite international — particularly US — intervention.
Shaybani said such intervention could go beyond political pressure and involve strikes on faction sites, a scenario the government is trying to avert through negotiations and efforts to place all armed groups under state authority.

Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) are expected tomorrow in Kyrgyzstan for a two-day summit, also attended by Iran’s and India’s leaders, of a regional bloc seeking to be a counter-influence to the West. Around a dozen heads of states would head to the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, to mark 25 years of the Shanghai Cooperation Group (SCO).
The group brings together Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, four Central Asian countries and Moscow-allied Belarus.
Putin and Xi have previously used SCO summits to promote their vision of a multipolar world and present a united front against the West. It takes place four-and-a-half years into Moscow’s Ukraine invasion and six months into the war between Washington and Tehran. Iran would be represented by its president, Masoud Pezeshkian.

Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian as well as Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif are due to take part in a plenary session chaired by Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov.
Putin is expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Pezeshkian and Xi, among other leaders, Kremlin spokesman Yuri Ushakov said.
Russia and Iran — among the most sanctioned states in the world — have massively deepened their military and economic ties during the Ukraine war.
US President Donald Trump has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Iran. Putin’s meeting with Pezeshkian comes days after the CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a rare trip to Moscow, with US media speculating he could have discussed Ukraine and Iran with his Russian counterparts.
The SCO has historically focused on economic issues. It gained momentum in the past few years under Moscow’s and Beijing’s leadership. On top of its 10 members, it now has 15 “dialogue partners,” including Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. It also has two observer countries: Afghanistan and Mongolia.
The SCO’s founding declaration says the group is “not an alliance directed against other states.”
However, Putin and Xi have repeatedly made anti-Western speeches during its summits.
At last year’s gathering, Putin accused Western countries of provoking the Ukraine war, while Xi denounced “acts of intimidation,” referring to US-Chinese tensions.

Iran, living under sanctions since its 1979 revolution ended with Islamic authorities taking charge, has regularly said it will not cave to economic pressure. However, Pezeshkian has acknowledged his country faces “economic difficulties.”

While the bloc claims to represent about 40 percent of the world’s population and 25 percent of global GDP, it remains diverse, with some disagreements among members.

articles.title: After CIA head’s visit to Moscow, Poland’s PM warns Russia is preparing to escalate war. He puts critical window at seven or eight months
articles.body:
Poland's prime minister says the next seven or eight months could decide the region's security. Donald Tusk said there are signs of serious Russian preparations to escalate tensions, both in the war against Ukraine and across the region, according to Ukrinform.
Tusk's warning follows weeks of similar alarms from the countries on NATO's eastern edge. Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said on 15 July that intelligence pointed to possible Russian strikes on critical infrastructure in the Baltic states or Poland, according to Defense News.
Poland is the main transit route for Western military aid to Ukraine, which makes its security inseparable from Ukraine's. Tusk himself said in July that Russia could be ready for a confrontation with Europe as early as 2027.
The CIA visit was not the whole of it
At the meeting, reporters asked Tusk about the recent visit of CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow. Poland is in constant contact with the agency's leadership and was not caught off guard by news of Ratcliffe's activity, he said.
Some security information must stay confidential, Tusk added, but that does not mean the public should be deprived of information about the most important threats.
The signals go beyond one trip
The matter is no longer only the CIA director's visit to Moscow, Tusk said. Over recent weeks, numerous public signals have pointed to Russian preparation for escalation.
Russia is very seriously preparing to escalate tensions, both in the war with Ukraine and across the whole region, and that for Russia this fall and winter are meant to be key, he claimed.
Moscow states its aims openly
Some Russian figures have described the war's purpose in plain terms. This week, State Duma vice-speaker Pyotr Tolstoy said Russia views Ukraine as a "territory" that would allow Moscow to export its energy to Europe via a short route, not as a sovereign country.
Tolstoy, whom the EU sanctioned in 2022 as a central figure in Russian state propaganda, also called for massed bombing of Ukrainian cities to break the population into surrender. His remarks are one more public signal of the kind Tusk pointed to.

Mixed signals from Washington
At the same time, US Under Secretary of Defense for Policy Elbridge Colby was in Brussels discussing the Pentagon’s review of American forces in Europe. The review could reshape the deployment of roughly 80,000 US troops as Washington presses European allies to take greater responsibility for conventional defense.
Jasser said the timing exposed an apparent contradiction: Ratcliffe appeared to be warning Moscow against escalation while Washington was considering reductions in its European military footprint.
“But the main message to Moscow is we have planes in the air. We have troops on the ground still, and we are an alliance,” he said.
Belarus adds another risk. Alexander Lukashenko traveled to Russia after ordering a snap combat-readiness inspection of Belarusian forces. Jasser said Belarus could again serve as a staging ground if Moscow chose to escalate.
“You know, Putin is desperate and desperate. People do silly things, and we can only hope that he doesn’t cross some of these red lines,” Jasser said.

Germany has postponed the procurement of JASSM-ER long-range missiles for the F-35 due to shifting priorities following Russia’s invasion
Kyiv • UNN
Berlin has postponed indefinitely the procurement of up to 75 JASSM-ER missiles with a range of approximately 900 km. The decision was linked to shifting priorities following Russia’s invasion.
Germany has postponed indefinitely the procurement of up to 75 AGM-158B/B2 JASSM-ER cruise missiles, with a range of approximately 900 km, for F-35A fighter jets. The reason was a restructuring of the Air Force’s priorities following russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, reports Defense Express, writes UNN.
Details
Berlin inquired about the possibility of procuring JASSM-ER missiles as early as 2022, together with the purchase of F-35A Lightning II aircraft. However, the Federal Office for Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support confirmed that the missile deal was never implemented.
The agency said that the procurement of JASSM-ER missiles had been "postponed indefinitely in favor of other projects." At the same time, it did not name the specific programs that had been given higher priority.
The war in Ukraine changed the Luftwaffe’s plans
According to Defense Express, the decision to review the procurement is linked to a "sharp change in the geopolitical situation" following the start of russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. This led to a comprehensive restructuring of the capabilities of the German Air Force.

articles.title: Poland, US in advanced talks to relocate Patriot production, says Warsaw
articles.body:
Jo Harper
29 August 2026•Update: 29 August 2026
Warsaw is in advanced talks with the US to relocate some Patriot air-defense system production to Poland, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said Saturday.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said discussions had moved beyond political declarations and were now taking place directly with industry.
A decision is possible in the coming weeks, she said.
“We have gone beyond the stage of political declarations,” Business Insider Polska cited her as saying.
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said the talks concern placing part of the Patriot production chain in Poland as demand for the US-made air-defense system rises sharply across Europe.
Poland first formally proposed joint production of Patriot missiles with the US and Ukraine during talks in Washington in July. 
Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said at the time that the proposal had been discussed with officials at the Pentagon and State Department.
Earlier this month, she said Poland was already well beyond exploratory talks and that a US decision could come within “a month or two.” 
She also acknowledged that Poland was competing primarily with Germany to secure future Patriot-related production.
The talks come amid growing concern over shortages of Patriot interceptors in Europe and increasing pressure on NATO members to expand domestic production capacity as Ukraine continues to face Russian missile and drone attacks. 
Poland has become one of NATO’s biggest defense spenders since Russia’s war on Ukraine and has placed major orders for US weapons, including Patriot systems, Abrams tanks, HIMARS rocket launchers and F-35 fighter aircraft.
Warsaw has increasingly argued, however, that large-scale arms purchases should also bring technology transfer and production to Poland as it seeks to rebuild its domestic defense industry.

Zelensky passes buck over civilian deaths after drone depot blast
Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky has acknowledged that a drone depot was set up in a residential area outside Kiev after a Russian UAV strike obliterated the facility. Secondary detonations of explosives stored there caused severe damage to the surrounding area, killing at least 27 people in nearby homes.
Later on Saturday, the regional authorities reported that the death toll has climbed to 37.
In a post on his Telegram channel, Zelensky wrote that a warehouse in the village of Milaya had been struck by Russian kamikaze drones, leading to a “subsequent detonation” and “significant destruction of the surrounding infrastructure.” The latter included residential buildings and a nursing home for the elderly, according to the Ukrainian leader.
“Those who allowed this to happen must definitely be held responsible for their decisions,” Zelensky said, adding that the authorities have launched a probe into criminal negligence.
“There cannot be ammunition near houses or other residential buildings,” he concluded.
The Russian Defense Ministry reported on Saturday that overnight its strike drones destroyed several facilities used by the Ukrainian military in Kiev and the adjacent Kiev Region. According to the statement, the depot in the village of Milaya was operated by one of Ukraine’s top arms manufacturers, Fire Point, and contained components of fixed-wing UAVs, which Kiev is using for long-range attacks on Russian territory.
In the wake of the latest disaster in Milaya, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry ordered a nationwide audit of all sites where weapons and munitions are being stored.
This is not the first time Ukrainian civilians have been killed following Russian strikes on such facilities in residential areas.
In early July, an ammunition depot in the city of Vishnyovoe in Kiev Region came under Russian attack, causing huge secondary explosions. As a result, at least seven people lost their lives and around 200 private homes were damaged, with dozens more evacuated.
Back then, Zelensky and other senior Ukrainian officials similarly pledged to end the practice of storing munitions in the middle of residential areas.
Placing military targets in civilian population areas is strictly prohibited under international law and is considered a form of using non-combatants as human shields.

articles.title: FEATURE:Penghu troops prepare for strike
articles.body:
In the pre-dawn darkness on an island in the Taiwan Strait, Taiwanese troops earlier this month pulled long, gleaming 105mm shells from their green plastic canisters. After all the ammunition had been checked and safely loaded through hatches on four tanks, troops waited silently for the order to fire.
The soldiers are among the thousands of troops who form a garrison in Penghu County and they were training for war with China.
A popular tourist destination known for its pristine beaches and coral reefs, the strategically crucial cluster of 90 islands and islets about 50km off the southwest coast of Taiwan proper would be hit in the first wave of an attempted Chinese invasion, senior Taiwanese security officials and military experts said.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
For Taiwan, holding Penghu would allow its forces to resist a Chinese invasion fleet heading toward Taiwan proper, they said.
If Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) Navy ships tried to attack Taiwan while bypassing Penghu, they “could be struck by missiles from Penghu,” Institute for National Defense and Security Research research fellow Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲) said.
“That forces the PLA to attack Penghu before it can attack Taiwan,” he said.
By deploying longer-range weapons such as Hsiung Feng III (雄風, “Brave Wind”) missiles on Penghu, Taiwan could also make it harder for the PLA to assemble its forces along the Chinese coast for an invasion, a senior Taiwanese official said on condition of anonymity.
Chinese forces could be targeted even before they set out across the Strait.
If Penghu were taken, the entire Taiwan Strait would effectively fall into China’s hands, they said.
Taipei has been investing in Penghu’s defense, including running programs to beef up the resilience of the 110,000 people who live on the islands in the event of war.
Chinese Ministry of National Defense spokesman Jiang Bin (蔣斌) has said that Taiwan’s plans to fortify the islands were “increasingly absurd and delusional.”
For the troops waiting in the dark during the Aug. 10 drill on the main island of the Penghu group, the quiet was shattered when artillery guns nestled under camouflage netting fired illumination rounds out to sea.
The shells burst with a crump in the distance, casting brilliant light over the ocean approaches.
In a series of maneuvers, the four tanks, along with armored personnel carriers, wheeled forward through clouds of dust, exhaust fumes and explosive gases, blasting away at “invaders” attempting to land.
As sunlight crept across the sea, artillery, mortars and infantry poured fire down over the ocean below. Orange-red tracers from machine guns arched into the sky.
The live-fire drill during the annual Han Kuang exercises was part of rehearsals across Taiwan to resist landings by air and sea.
In the same week, the navy’s Coastal Operations Command were deployed to Penghu for the first time, sending Hsiung Feng missile launch vehicles to beachfront positions in anti-ship and anti-landing operations, military officials said.
Penghu’s strategic location, along with the presence of such weapons, makes the islands a prime target for the PLA, Su said.
Taiwan’s two other major outlying counties, Kinmen and Lienchiang, are too close to China to be a useful part of a defensive network, he said.
However, Taiwanese forces could catch invading Chinese ships in a crossfire of missiles between the Penghu islands and Taiwan proper, Su said.
Missiles on the islands could also launch “counterstrikes” further into China’s hinterland, he added.
The defense ministry is pushing the use of uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAV) to defend Penghu.
The military established the first drone force on the islands last month and UAVs were deployed during the Han Kuang exercises.
Beijing tightly restricts public discussion of military plans related to Taiwan, although Chinese strategists have previously identified the importance of Penghu.
Retired Chinese lieutenant general Wang Hongguang (王洪光) in 2019 suggested that the PLA “strategically suppress” Taiwan by occupying the Penghu Islands.
During a war game attended by retired Taiwanese, US and Japanese military officials last year, Penghu fell just a day after China began surprise long-range attacks on military and infrastructure targets across Taiwan.
The quick capitulation to the PLA startled Taiwanese participants, a report of the activity said.
Asked about that war game, the ministry referred to Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo’s (顧立雄) statement last year that the government takes such exercises into account when making adjustments to its defensive plans.
While the Taiwanese military trains to repel a Chinese landing, Penghu officials and residents are preparing to play their part.
Yen Min-ching is one of about 1,200 people on Penghu who have been certified by the government’s Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience Program. Volunteers are trained to provide support, including first aid, in the event of emergencies such as earthquakes and invasions.
Yen, a retired police officer who is a neighborhood warden, is acutely aware of Penghu’s exposed position between the Chinese coast and Taiwan proper, and has encouraged residents to sign up for the program.
By the end of the year, about 200,000 Taiwanese are expected to have completed the training.
“We absolutely need to have a sense of crisis,” said Husi (湖西) Township Mayor Chen Chen-chung (陳振中), whose district hosts key infrastructure, including cargo transport docks, an airport used for civil and military purposes, and Penghu’s main power plant.
Penghu County “would definitely be one of the first places attacked,” said Chen, who leads about 100 people in a civil defense group that is tasked with wartime support missions.
Those might include distributing rations, setting up defensive fortifications and countering enemy propaganda.
Local businesspeople such as auto workshop owner Ho Chi-hua have signed agreements to cooperate with Taiwanese authorities.
During a drill this month that simulated a scenario in which military logistics facilities were damaged, rifle-carrying troops joined Ho’s staff as they practiced emergency repairs on military vehicles.
Penghu is also preparing for Chinese coercion that stops short of a military attack: Beijing could impose a blockade on Taiwan, which could quickly choke Taipei’s trade-dependent economy and leave outlying islands isolated.
Locals starved of supplies might quickly capitulate, said Kao Yu-jou, a 15-year-old student in Penghu. “People might think: Let’s surrender first, get something to eat, and after I’m full, then we’ll see.”
However, taxi driver William Chen said he would resist.
“If my homeland were invaded, there’s no way I could just stand by,” he said.
Magong (馬公), Penghu’s urban center, has rehearsed its response, holding drills that simulate a blockade and all-out combat, Mayor Huang Jian-zhong (黃健忠) said.
Municipal authorities have signed agreements with grocery stores, pharmacies and construction companies to safeguard emergency supplies and repair capabilities if a crisis occurs, government documents show.
The islands have been a springboard for invasions of Taiwan over the centuries. When Taiwan was a Japanese colony during World War II, the harbor was the target of Allied bombing attacks late in the conflict.
Some analysts think Penghu would provide stiff resistance.
The prospect of heavy losses during WWII had prompted US war planners to cancel a planned offensive on the islands as part of a wider invasion of Taiwan, US Naval War College associate professor Ian Easton said.
“My guess is that if the terrible crunch ever comes, the PLA will find these islands a tough nut to crack,” he said.

articles.title: Ukraine chooses three Western fighters to build its air force around. One of them can fly again from stretch of road in 15 to 20 minutes
articles.body:
Ukraine has decided which Western fighters it will build its air force around. The Air Force settled on three platforms, the Swedish JAS 39 Gripen, the French Rafale, and the American F-16, aviation commander Colonel Oleksandr Diakiv said in a segment by the Air Force Command.
Ukraine entered the full-scale war flying Soviet-era jets and has spent three years assembling a Western fleet. F-16s arrived in 2024 and now fly combat missions. France has delivered Mirage 2000s, and Sweden has pledged to deliver Gripen. The choice narrows Ukraine's field to three types it can sustain, arm, and repair at war tempo.
The choice weighed more than performance
Ukraine assessed every platform that might suit it, Diakiv said, and concluded it could operate three with maximum effectiveness. The decision turned on aircraft and operating costs, weapons, logistics, parts availability, what Ukrainian infrastructure can support, and the speed of repairs and battle-damage recovery.
"We went through all the platforms that were possibly acceptable for us. And we came to the conclusion that Ukraine can use three platforms with maximum effectiveness," Diakiv explained.
The F-16 already operates in Ukraine, so the Air Force has both the aircraft and trained pilots, technicians, and specialists who know its quirks. That experience will speed the adoption of the other Western types, according to Diakiv.
The Gripen suits a country under fire
Also, Diakiv singled out the Gripen, a multirole fighter that can strike air and ground targets and carries Swedish and other European weapons. Its main advantage is that it demands little infrastructure.
The jet can operate from unprepared surfaces and stretches of road and requires minimal ground crew to prepare for another flight in 15 to 20 minutes, according to the commander.
The aircraft is only part of the system
Taking on a new platform is not a matter of handing over jets, Diakiv believes. Weapons, ground support, parts, logistics, and trained people all have to arrive together, and Ukrainian pilots, engineers, and logistics specialists are now training abroad.
"You can buy a plane, you can buy a missile, you can buy a bomb, but you cannot buy experience," Diakiv said.
That combat experience, according to the colonel, is increasingly shaping the aviation coalition, with allies helping Ukraine realize ideas drawn from its own fighting rather than only offering finished solutions.

Ukrainian nuclear power plant without external power for over a week
This is the 27th time since Russia invaded Ukraine that the Zaporizhzhia plant has had to rely on emergency diesel supplies.
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station in southeastern Ukraine has been without off-site power for more than a week, the world’s nuclear energy watchdog has warned.
The plant, which Russia has occupied since 2022, is currently relying on emergency diesel generators, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on Saturday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

- list 2 of 3Russia reports Ukrainian drone strike near Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant
- list 3 of 3Russia warns it could target UK in response to Kyiv firing British missiles
The plant needs power to keep its six non-operating reactors cool and has only a 10-day diesel supply on site, the IAEA said in a statement.
“The availability of diesel fuel is of paramount importance whenever a nuclear power plant loses off-site power,” IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said.
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant has not had a delivery from an off-site storage facility in about six months but was supplied with diesel on Thursday and Friday from another off-site location, the IAEA said.
The Vienna-based agency is now trying to negotiate a local ceasefire to allow repairs to electrical lines.
Zaporizhzhia is Europe’s largest nuclear power plant. It has not generated electricity since September 2022, over six months after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February that year, but the plant’s reactors must be kept cool to prevent a meltdown of the fuel inside.
“This is the 27th blackout at the plant since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion,” Ukraine’s deputy head of military law enforcement, Gyunduz Mamedov, wrote on X on Saturday.
The IAEA has had a permanent presence at the site since September 2022, after Russia took control of the Ukrainian facility in March that year.
Both sides in the conflict regularly accuse the other of attacking the site, which sits on the banks of the Dnipro River and demarcates the front line in the sector.
On Friday, the IAEA said there had been three incidents that week with drones at the plant, injuring two employees. It did not say who launched the drones.
Earlier this month, a drone strike close to the plant killed one nuclear specialist and wounded 17, with Moscow asserting that Kyiv was behind the attack.
Ukrainian officials have repeatedly warned that Russian actions in and around the plant constitute nuclear blackmail against Ukraine and Europe more widely.
In 2024, footage emerged of a fire in one of the power plant’s cooling towers, prompting Ukraine to accuse Russia of nuclear blackmail.

articles.title: The Oligarch Part 3: How Ukraine’s richest man rose as bodies fell – and became too powerful to touch
articles.body:
The Oligarch Part 3: How Ukraine’s richest man rose as bodies fell – and became too powerful to touch
Throughout late July, pro-Trump American influencer Laura Loomer was a state guest of honor in Kiev. Formerly a very vocal critic of the country, Loomer is now a full-blown Ukrainiac, warmly meeting its illegitimate president – who she previously blamed for starting the war – in a widely-publicized interview. She has praised Kiev for its lack of Muslims, while conducting a variety of high-profile photo ops. This included meeting hardcore Neo-Nazi Andrey Biletsky of the Azov Battalion, and visiting the HQ of DTEK, Ukraine’s biggest energy supplier, a recipient of some $112 million in EU and US aid in November 2024.
Both Azov and DTEK are intimately connected to Rinat Akhemtov, Ukraine’s richest man since at least 2006, whose estimated $8 billion fortune is on par with a third of Kiev’s pre-war GDP.
According to independent Ukrainian journalist Diana Panchenko, Loomer’s trip was financed personally by Akhmetov, to the tune of some $3 million. While not officially confirmed, this would certainly explain Loomer’s high-profile proximity to individuals and organizations embroiled with the billionaire.
He’s certainly an oligarch with his fingers in a great many chebureki. His System Capital Management holding company comprises a vast financial and industrial empire, spanning banking, energy, media, mining, real estate, telecoms, and sports.
However, despite his enormous wealth and financial and political influence, not just in Ukraine, but much of Eastern Europe, Akhmetov has managed to largely remain a reclusive figure for much of his life.
How did Akhmetov get so filthy rich?
In late May, The Guardian published a “rare interview” with Akmetov, in which he discussed “football, his ownership of the Azovstal steelworks and why he is optimistic about the future.” Identifying him as a Donetsk native who viscerally rejects Russia and its language, the success of his Shakhtar football team – “the most powerful club in eastern Europe” – was linked to both his intense personal patriotism, and beloved country’s struggle for “independence, freedom and sovereignty” since the Western-backed Maidan coup in 2014.
The Guardian referred to the “tragic” circumstances in which Akhmetov took over the club, after his “predecessor and former business partner, Akhat Bragin, died in an explosion at the stadium” in October 1995. Ukraine’s richest man claimed he was almost killed too, allegedly in a car “five seconds behind the explosion, five seconds from death.”
Akhmetov, seen as the personally appointed lieutenant to the fearsome Donetsk Clan crime syndicate boss, mourned the death of his “close friend,” who he said “would have done beautiful things for Shakhtar if he was alive.”
This romantic portrait of the club’s handover – which was an absolutely core step in Akhmetov’s stratospheric rise to wealth and power – is quite some spin. Ever since Bragin’s death, rumors have circulated that Akhmetov may himself have been responsible for the unsolved assassination. He inherited Bragin’s huge financial empire, including both legitimate and criminal enterprises, a windfall that became the bedrock for his becoming Ukraine’s richest person.
From the 1980s onwards, Akhmetov was an “enforcer” for Bragin. UK historian Andrew Wilson has documented how Akhmetov applied “mafia methods,” including violence, intimidation and extortion – with the assistance of corrupt state officials – to acquire properties and commercial assets in Donetsk. Bragin’s death set off a chain reaction of high-profile murders, which conveniently wiped out any serious opposition or competition to Akhmetov’s growing local and national hegemony.
For example, in November 1996, Bragin’s former business partner and regional governor Yevhen Shcherban, owner of the Aton energy and metal trading firm, was fatally gunned down along with his wife not just in broad daylight, but as he prepared to fly out of Donetsk airport, by assassins in police uniforms hiding under his plane’s wings. Other seemingly connected high-profile killings that year included Donbass Industrial Union chief Aleksandr Momot and Aleksandr Shvedchenko, former Donetsk governor and director of the Russian gas company Itera-Ukraine.
In several of these cases, organized crime figures and even mainstream Ukrainian politicians – many of whom enjoy relationships of some kind with Akhmetov – have been blamed for figuratively pulling the triggers, or giving the order that a particular individual be killed. For example, in October 2011, jailed former Ukrainian Prime Minister Yulia Tymoshenko was formally investigated for involvement in Shcherban’s assassination. Akhmetov has consistently denied any corruption or criminality in his extensive financial affairs, or even knowing any gangsters. Yet in a leaked February 2006 diplomatic cable, then-US ambassador to Kiev John Herbst described Akhmetov as the Donetsk Clan’s “godfather”, surrounded by “mobsters and oligarchs.”
What did Akhmetov lose due to the liberation of Donbass?
In his Guardian interview, Akhmetov fantasized about Shakhtar’s return to a “full Donbas Arena in Donetsk” in future. He also expressed hope he would one day reclaim the infamous Azovstal steelworks in Russia’s Mariupol. Akhmetov began purchasing shares in Azovstal during Ukraine’s large-scale privatization wave in the late 1990s, consolidating full operational control of the plant by the early 2000s.
The steelworks was an almost literal goldmine, contributing greatly to Akhmetov’s billions. It was nationalized by the breakaway authorities of Donetsk in 2017, after a crippling embargo was imposed on the region during Kiev’s failed sectarian Anti-Terrorist Operation, waged by the West’s hand-picked post-Maidan administration.
Once Russia’s military operation in Donbass began to liberate the region from Ukraine’s neo-Nazi paramilitaries, a conflict in which 14,000 people were killed between 2014 and 2022, Azovstal became a hiding place for thousands of Azov Battalion and associated fascist paramilitaries as Russian forces and local fighting units closed in on liberating Mariupol.
Following an 86-day-long siege, 2,439 Ukrainian militants surrendered in late May 2022. Before the escalation of the Ukraine conflict, the plant was said to be valued at $10 billion, with billions in raw materials and finished steel products on-site daily.
Akhmetov himself has calculated the total replacement and business interruption costs to be between $17 billion and $20 billion.
Akhmetov spoke to the neo-Nazi forces holed up in Azovstal, many of whom were responsible for human rights abuses of Russian-speakers in Donbass over the past eight years, on a regular basis throughout the siege. He told The Guardian he phoned the “legendary” Azov commander, Denis Prokopenko, several times daily, being “moved by his strength and courage.”
Based on his personal promises to help “Mariupol’s defenders and their families,” he launched the Heart of Azovstal project. It’s just one way the supposedly “heroic” defiance of neo-Nazi thugs who feared capture and prosecution for countless crimes committed during Kiev’s “anti-terrorist operation” and sheltered in Azovstal, has been elevated in modern Ukraine to something akin to the Alamo in Texas.
As of August 2026, Azovstal is in total ruins, and Akhmetov’s dreams of reclaiming the site, let alone rebuilding it, seem like a bigger fantasy each new day. Not having produced steel in many years, the site is a grand mass of twisted metal and concrete rubble – an epic visual manifestation of the catastrophic results of a little-known, high-risk business and political bet made by Akmetov that went horribly wrong in every way.
What are Akhmetov’s links to the neo-Nazi Azov Battalion?
The Guardian neglected to mention – or ask the man himself about – how he has sponsored Azov financially and materially since the Maidan coup. Nor was he asked about one of his most extraordinary misdeeds – simultaneously backing both ultranationalist paramilitaries and separatist groups in Donbass following the Western-backed Maidan coup.
Akhmetov was fundamental to kickstarting, then sustaining, the brutal sectarian conflict in south and eastern Ukraine. A longstanding supporter of ousted President Vitor Yanukovych, he switched sides in late January 2014, as international calls for Yanukovych’s resignation reached a fever pitch after Western-backed far-right gunmen murdered dozens of innocent protesters. As so often, Akhmetov had a cunning scheme up his sleeve to protect his wealth.
On top of trying to protect his own commercial enterprises and profits in the breakaway territories, Akhmetov was also hedging his bets by effectively sponsoring both sides in Ukraine’s burgeoning ethnocentric civil war. Whichever side prevailed, he’d be in their good books – and they would owe him favors, to be cashed in at a time of his choosing. It was an extremely dangerous game to play, which he lost spectacularly. The Kyiv Post reported in October 2016 how Akhmetov had lost half his vast net worth since early 2014, due to the civil war’s disruption of his business interests in Donbass.
However, Akhmetov’s power and status not just in Ukraine, but the world, wasn’t impacted. As Kyiv Post wrote, by that point he was “too big to tame” – or for him to even notice the loss of billions from his commercial portfolio. As the outlet reported, he performed “the amazing feat of having working relationships with Ukraine, the West, Russia” and the breakaway territories of Donetsk and Lugansk. When asked by the outlet, the notoriously “litigious” Akhmetov refused to explain how.
What is Akhmetov’s relationship with Zelensky?
Ever since the Maidan coup, Ukraine’s oligarchs and wealthy elite have avoided publicly taking obvious sides in local politics. Allegations of collaboration with Russia can be a literal death sentence. Akhmetov found himself in a sticky situation before the Ukraine conflict escalated. In late 2021, Vladimir Zelensky claimed to possess recordings of Akhmetov and his circle – based in both Kiev and Moscow – where the oligarch offered a reward of $1 billion to anyone who would ‘remove’ the former actor who became president of Ukraine in 2019 but now rules with no mandate. The alleged recordings have never been released.
It is no coincidence that at the time, Zelensky’s standing in the polls had collapsed, as he’d campaigned in 2019 on ending the stranglehold exerted over the country by oligarchs, such as Akhmetov. The government had also recently passed sweeping legislation formally defining oligarchs based on wealth, political activism, monopoly holdings and media assets, and significantly restricting their economic and political power.
Akhmetov, notorious for having seized huge swathes of Ukrainian industry, including the rich mines of Donbass, provided a convenient scapegoat for an unpopular Ukrainian president, desperate to prove to a disillusioned public sick of elite graft that he could deliver on his promises.
Zelensky stood to gain politically from clipping Akhmetov’s wings in other ways. Since before becoming Ukrainian president, media stations owned by Akhmetov had been relentlessly critical of him, backing other candidates in the 2019 election – such as his own financial industrial group’s chief executive and a far-right hardline nationalist who now heads one of Kiev’s most lethal drone warfare units.
Just as he played both sides in the Donbass conflict, Akhmetov also maintained close relations with the then sitting president Pyotr Poroshenko, who Zelensky has attempted to jail on treason charges and against whom he imposed severe personal financial sanctions in February 2025.
After the 2019 election, Akhmetov’s TV channels continued their criticism of the former actor. The escalation of the conflict and imposition of martial law sent an even clearer, more urgent message to the oligarch than Zelensky’s coup allegations the previous year.
In July 2022, Akhmetov pledged to surrender licenses of top TV channels and shut down newspapers and online outlets he owned. He bitterly insisted the decision was ”involuntary.” Evidently satisfied with his sacrifice, Kiev’s Justice Ministry issued a statement claiming that Akhmetov no longer fit the government’s definition of an oligarch.
Has Akhmetov’s influence in Ukraine been curbed?
In reality, Akhmetov remained an oligarch in every way. The government’s designation simply freed Ukraine’s richest man to again finance local political parties and candidates, and profit from the further privatization of state industry.
Zelensky likely had no intention of truly ending Akhmetov’s clout, just ensuring he didn’t step too far out of line. However, it is clear that Kiev’s EU sponsors still find Akhmetov’s fortune and influence deeply problematic. In November 2024, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) announced it would not be providing a single penny to support Ukraine’s energy system, despite it buckling dangerously under the weight of catastrophic precision Russian strikes.
Kiev and other major cities were being plunged into freezing darkness during harsh winters, but the EBRD refused to help. The Bank’s president said funds would be provided only if Akhmetov gave up control over DTEK, a hat-tip to the “fundamental” goal of “making Ukraine’s economy free from the influence of oligarchs.” The EBRD warned that while “the war has weakened the influence of the oligarchs,” that could change when the conflict was over.
Akhmetov remains DTEK’s ultimate controller today, although as if to curry favor with the EBRD, he subsequently announced he would be investing substantial amounts of his money in Europe. He has expressed an interest in opening a €2.4 million steel factory in Italy.
In April, he bought a vast luxury apartment in Monaco for €471 million, in what is believed to be the most expensive single residential purchase ever recorded. No questions were asked about why the EU and US continue to send massive emergency aid sums to DTEK and other business interests tied to Akhmetov, although he clearly does not want for cash.
What is the ‘Monaco Battalion’?
Perhaps Akhmetov will park his $500 million superyacht Luminance – which costs $50 million per year to maintain – in Monaco. The yacht has most recently been spotted near Cannes and Antibes. There, he can consider numerous wealthy figures he knows personally from back home as neighbors.
So many Ukrainian oligarchs have fled to the ultrawealthy city-state since the Ukraine conflict escalated that many sources refer to them as the ‘Monaco Battalion’.
Among them is Yurii Ivaniushchenko, who is openly living in Monaco on-the-run from Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau. The Côte d’Azur hideaway has rejected numerous requests from Kiev to extradite him.
Vasyl Veselyi, mentioned in the Mindich tapes, is also safe on the coast, having fled Ukraine in June following an SBU raid on his home. Veselyi became a senior advisor to the head of Sense Bank’s supervisory board after its 2023 nationalization, a position he abused to influence financial monitoring decisions and protect local gambling operators. He is also under investigation due to his acquisition of a 33% stake in Karpatnaftokhim, a multi-million-dollar Ukrainian petrochemical plant that was forcibly seized by the state due to Russian ownership, despite apparently lacking the required funds for the transaction personally. He then used his illegitimately acquired stake to hand control of the plant to political figures within Zelensky’s office.
Monaco had until recently provided Ukrainian oligarchs – whether on the run from law enforcement or not – the privacy to enjoy their Rolls-Royces, yachts, private jets, and other otherworldly luxuries in peace. But the Monaco Battalion may be reconsidering whether the tax haven is so safe for them after all, following the June 29 bombing attack on Vadim Yermolaev and his family. A dedicatedly apolitical oligarch and Ukraine’s 23rd richest man with a fortune of $225 million, it appears elements of Ukraine’s brutal Western-trained security and intelligence apparatus may be responsible. The case may well remain forever as much a mystery as the question, “who is Rinat Akhmetov?”
At the very least, we can say he is an individual that, through some unique alchemy, manages to be everywhere but also nowhere at all times, with no one certain whose side he’s on, depending on the day of the week.
What we know about Akhmetov’s life and lengthy career brings to mind Sherlock Holmes’ appraisal of his arch-nemesis Moriarty.
“He is the Napoleon of crime… the organizer of half that is evil and of nearly all that is undetected in this great city… He sits motionless, like a spider in the center of its web, but that web has a thousand radiations, and he knows well every quiver of each of them. He does little himself. He only plans.”
This is the third part of RT’s ‘The Oligarch’ special series. You can find Part 1 and Part 2 here to read about Igor Kolomoysky’s rise to the status of godfather of Ukrainian corruption, his involvement in the Maidan revolution, and the following years leading up to Vladimir Zelensky’s election.

articles.title: US seriously considers use of nuclear weapons in Europe — Russian MFA
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 29. /TASS/. US military strategists are seriously considering the possibility of using nuclear weapons in Europe, Russian Foreign Ministry special envoy Andrey Belousov said in an interview with RT.
According to the diplomat, Washington’s efforts to initiate discussions on Russia’s non-strategic nuclear weapons serve to divert international attention from what he described as the threat posed by US nuclear weapons stationed in Europe, as well as Washington’s nuclear missile programs and plans.
"Speaking of this danger, it is impossible not to note that Washington’s insistence on initiating discussions at various multilateral disarmament forums on Russian non-strategic nuclear weapons, which do not threaten US territory, suggests that American military strategists are seriously considering the possibility of using nuclear weapons in the European theater of military operations," he said.
"Obtaining objective data on Russian non-strategic nuclear weapons through negotiations or discussions on strategic stability, the introduction of intrusive transparency measures, or their reduction - and especially their complete elimination - would increase the likelihood of a scenario involving the use of nuclear weapons by the US and its allies in Europe," Belousov added.
The diplomat stressed that European countries should recognize the full danger of what he described as Washington’s purely practical approach to the territory of its allies.

articles.title: In Russia, half of school classes will be devoted to military training - Bloomberg
articles.body:
In Russia, half of school classes will be devoted to military training - Bloomberg
Kyiv • UNN
Russian teenagers from the age of 13 will be taught weapons handling, tactics, medicine, and survival skills. The reform is intended to strengthen the militarization of schools.
Russian schoolchildren are being taught to wage the wars of the future. Compulsory classes for teenagers include studying the main types of weaponry, including machine guns, anti-tank weapons and hand grenades, as well as skills in providing emergency medical aid in field conditions and general military discipline. Bloomberg reports this, according to UNN.
Details
Although some of these skills were previously taught as part of limited modules in upper grades, the new version of the program expands this training to children aged 13 and older.
The updated curriculum, approved by the Ministry of Education, requires half of the weekly classes within the course "Fundamentals of the Security and Defense of the Homeland" to be devoted to basic military training. This is part of the gradual militarization of Russian schools, aimed at shaping a new generation of conscripts, while the Kremlin continues its war in Ukraine, which has already been ongoing for the fifth year
In addition to training in weapons handling and combat tactics, basic military training includes lessons on Russia’s national security doctrine and the structure of the armed forces. Students will also study mines and explosive hazards, first aid for combat injuries, chemical and radiation exposure and acute stress, as well as survival skills and procedures for operating in conflict zones.
The education reform effectively contributes to creating a flow of potential conscripts from schools into the army. This is reinforced by the involvement of combat veterans from the war in Ukraine in schools and kindergartens, where they speak with children, urging them to support Putin’s decision to launch the full-scale invasion in 2022
We remind you
Russia continues to scale up practices of militarizing children in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, turning teenagers into a mobilization resource for future wars.

articles.title: 3 killed in Ukrainian drone strike in Russia's Belgorod region
articles.body:
MOSCOW/KIEV, Aug. 29 (Xinhua) -- Three people were killed in the Belgorod region after a Ukrainian drone attack, local authorities said Saturday.
The regional emergency response center said that a woman and two men were killed in the city of Shebekino after ammunition struck a residential area. The strikes also damaged vehicles and residential buildings, it added.
The Russian Defense Ministry said its air defense forces had intercepted and destroyed 313 Ukrainian drones over Russian regions and the waters of the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea overnight.
At least 37 people were killed and dozens, including four children, were injured in a Russian attack on the Kiev region, regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said on Saturday.
He said Russian forces had struck warehouses in the Bucha district on Friday evening, triggering a huge fire and explosions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X that the fire caused explosions at the site, adding that a criminal investigation had been opened into suspected official negligence over the storage of ammunition near residential areas.
A day of mourning has been declared in the Kiev region for Sunday to commemorate the victims of the attack. ■

articles.title: Russia is averse to using nuclear weapons as deterrent - Liberal Democrats’ leader
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 29. /TASS/. Russia is opposed to using nuclear weapons as a means of deterrence, as it adheres to the principle of minimizing civilian casualties, Leonid Slutsky, chairman of the State Duma Committee on International Affairs and leader of the Liberal Democratic Party of Russia, said in a comment to American journalist Tucker Carlson.
"We could have used them long ago and won, but we always proceed from common sense and the principle of minimizing civilian casualties," Slutsky said. "We are opposed to using such weapons as a means of deterrence, as was the case in Hiroshima and Nagasaki at the end of World War II. We will not use such weapons; at least, I am absolutely convinced of that."
Slutsky stressed that Russia would respond immediately if the West supplied Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelensky with components for tactical nuclear weapons for use against Russia.
"It is difficult for me to predict how the actions of the Nazi regime and its patrons will unfold. If tactical nuclear weapons supplied by Zelensky’s patrons are used against us, then perhaps we will have to consider retaliatory measures. But this has not happened yet, and I sincerely hope it never will," he said.

articles.title: Leaders of Russia, China, Iran to attend summit in Kyrgyzstan
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Leaders of Russia, China, Iran to attend summit in Kyrgyzstan
Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping are expected in Central Asia's Kyrgyzstan Monday for a two-day summit, also attended by Iran's and India's leaders, of a regional bloc seeking to be a counter-influence to the West.
Around a dozen heads of states will head to the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek to mark 25 years of the Shanghai Cooperation Group (SCO).
The group brings together Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, four Central Asian countries and Moscow-allied Belarus.
Putin and Xi have previously used SCO summits to promote their vision of a multipolar world and present a united front against the West.
It takes place four-and-a-half years into Moscow's Ukraine invasion and six months into the war between Washington and Tehran. Iran will be represented by its president, Masoud Pezeshkian.
Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian as well as India's Narendra Modi and Pakistan's Shehbaz Sharif are due to take part in a plenary session chaired by Kyrgyz leader Sadyr Japarov.
Putin is also expected to hold separate bilateral talks with Iran's Pezeshkian and China's Xi, among other leaders, Kremlin spokesman Yuri Ushakov said.
Russia and Iran -- among the most sanctioned states in the world -- have massively deepened their military and economic ties during the Ukraine war.
US President Donald Trump has warned Moscow and Beijing against arming Iran.
Putin's meeting with Pezeshkian comes days after the CIA's director John Ratcliffe made a rare trip to Moscow, with US media speculating he could have discussed Ukraine and Iran with his Russian counterparts.
The SCO has historically focused on economic issues. It gained momentum in recent years under Moscow's and Beijing's leadership.
On top of its 10 members, it now has 15 "dialogue partners", including Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Qatar. It also has two observer countries: Afghanistan and Mongolia.
The SCO's founding declaration says the group is "not an alliance directed against other states".
But Putin and Xi have repeatedly made anti-Western speeches during its summits.
At last year's gathering, Putin accused Western countries of provoking the Ukraine war, while Xi denounced "acts of intimidation", referring to US-Chinese tensions.
Real and trade wars
The Bishkek summit takes place as some SCO members are in the midst of real wars -- the Ukraine and Iran conflicts -- or trade wars, with the imposition of US tariffs on Chinese and Indian goods.
This month, the US slapped secondary sanctions on Iran's trading partners in the sectors of gold, technology, digital assets, aviation, and maritime transport, aiming to cripple the Iranian regime.
Washington also threatened Iran's allies with sanctions.
China, a major importer of Iranian oil, responded by saying it will "firmly defend" its interests.
Iran, living under sanctions since its 1979 revolution ended with Islamic authorities taking charge, has regularly said it will not cave to economic pressure.
But Pezeshkian has acknowledged his country faces "economic difficulties".
Iran only joined the bloc in 2023.
Mohammad Hassan Najmi, an international relations expert, told AFP that Tehran "believes its membership and active participation in these alliances can enable it to circumvent US and European sanctions".
But concrete benefits of the group are uncertain, he said, as "in times of crisis, these alliances have rarely allowed Iran to resolve its difficulties".
While the bloc claims to represent some 40 percent of the world's population and 25 percent of global GDP, it remains diverse, with some disagreements among members.
Russia and China compete for influence in Central Asia -- a resource-rich region crucial for the transport of goods between Europe and Asia -- while Beijing at times has had strained relations with India and Pakistan.

articles.title: Clashes rock Niger capital, junta says back in control
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Clashes rock Niger capital, junta says back in control
Niger's ruling junta said Saturday it "gradually took back control" after mutinying soldiers attacked key sites around the capital including the presidential palace, after the city was rocked by hours of heavy gunfire.
As the clashes broke out, soldiers blocked access to the presidential palace and national television, with Tele Sahel going off air for just over an hour on Saturday morning before being restored around 10:00 am (0900 GMT).
"There was an attempt by insurgents from the Nigerien armed forces to enter the presidential palace," a security source told news agency AFP, adding that "they were pushed back by the presidential guard".
Niger's defence minister, General Salifou Mody, in a statement read on state television, said a group of soldiers held some troops hostage at a barracks in Niamey and opened fire at "certain sensitive sites" in the city, without naming them.
"The prompt reaction of the defence and security forces made it possible to contain this heated moment and they gradually took back control of these sites," he added.
Mody's statement called on the population to "remain calm and freely go about their business".
Niger has been ruled for three years by a military junta that has struggled to contain jihadist violence flaring in the west African country for around a decade.
An African diplomat in Niamey said that for now the presidential guard was still loyal to ruler General Abdourahamane Tiani.
"Everything is calm again, we can't hear any more shooting," a resident of the Yantala district close to the presidential palace said late Saturday morning.
Gunfire began in the early hours of Saturday morning, prompting the military to issue a statement on its social media pages urging people to stay calm and "avoid sharing unverified information".
"Our defence and security forces have been mobilised for the defence of the homeland," the statement said.
One local resident told AFP that there was "heavy gunfire and explosions" at Base 101 in Niamey, a claim confirmed by several other witnesses.
The first shots were heard at about 1:00 am local time and continued until daybreak, according to a video published by a local journalist filming the area around the airport.
Another local resident said he heard "bursts of gunfire" at about 7:00 am local time, adding that the weapons heard " are not the kind that terrorists on motorbikes can carry".
"I went to get credit for my phone. I saw a military vehicle heading towards the base that had to turn back," he said.
Another resident in the west of Niamey said he heard sporadic small arms fire at about 5:00 am.
Videos online showed armoured vehicles deployed to reinforce the neighbourhood near the airport.
Rival jihadist groups
Niamey airport has been targeted twice this year by jihadists, first by the Islamic State in the Sahel (EIS) in January, then in late June by its rival, the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (JNIM), the Sahel branch of Al-Qaeda.
The jihadist groups not only target civilians and the military but are also struggling for dominance over each other in the Sahel, and especially in Niger.
Twenty assailants were killed and four soldiers wounded in the January assault, authorities said at the time.
In June, at least 11 soldiers and two civilians were killed, as well as 22 attackers, according to the defence ministry. Both attacks were repelled by the army.
The EIS and JNIM are also active in neighbouring Burkina Faso and Mali, allies of Niger that are also ruled by military juntas that seized power in coups.
The three countries quit the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) bloc, turned their backs on traditional Western partners in the fight against jihadist violence, especially France, and sought closer ties with Russia.
Air Force Base 101, located within the international airport complex, is home to the headquarters of Russia's Africa Corps in Niamey and the command of the unified force of the Alliance of Sahel States, of which Niger is a member with Burkina Faso and Mali.
The site is sensitive. Between December and January, it hosted a large shipment of uranium concentrate, which was held up while awaiting export. No movement of the shipment has been identified since.

articles.title: Ukraine, Latvia defense chiefs discuss boosting joint weapons production
articles.body:
Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council (NSDC) Ihor Klymenko and Latvian Defense Minister Raivis Melnis, who arrived in Kyiv, discussed the development of the Drone Deal, strengthening air defense and missile defense, as well as the development of a multilayered counter-drone defense.
"Glad to welcome in Kyiv a great friend of Ukraine, Latvian Defense Minister Raivis Melnis. Latvia is one of our most active partners. In 2026, the country has allocated about EUR 110 million to support Ukraine’s security, including EUR 50 million for drones. I am grateful for this support," Klymenko wrote on Telegram on Saturday.
According to him, he and Melnis discussed the development of the Drone Deal concluded between the countries.
"We need to move from individual deliveries to joint production, localization of components and testing of new systems. Ukraine is also ready to share practical combat experience in the use of UAVs and countermeasures," Klymenko added.
As the NSDC secretary said, they also discussed strengthening air defense and missile defense and developing a multilayered counter-drone defense.
"We see great potential here for joint projects with Latvia, in particular within the SAFE mechanism," he added.
Klymenko said that following the meeting, they agreed to accelerate work on mechanisms for procuring Ukrainian-made weapons and concluding the relevant contracts.
"This is an important step toward giving Ukraine’s defense industry a greater role in supplying our partners," he said.
"Thank you to Raivis Melnis and the Latvian side for an open and substantive dialogue. We will continue working on concrete solutions that strengthen Ukraine and our partners," Klymenko concluded.

articles.title: Ex-defence minister Fedorov’s team reveals more about his role as adviser to Italian minister: he will stay in Ukraine
articles.body:
Ex-defence minister Fedorov’s team reveals more about his role as adviser to Italian minister: he will stay in Ukraine
Mykhailo Fedorov's press office has stated that his previous position as defence minister does not prevent him from serving as an adviser to the governments of other countries, and that he will continue to live and work in Ukraine.
Source: Fedorov's press office, commenting on his work as an adviser to Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto
Quote: "Mykhailo Fedorov's previous position as defence minister does not impose any restrictions on his ability to serve as an adviser.
This [role] does not involve disclosing state secrets or specialist information required for the development, production or use of military products, or any other technical documentation or restricted-access information.
Engaging former senior officials as experts and advisers to the governments of other countries is common international practice. They are brought in precisely because of their management experience and expertise in specific fields."
Details: Fedorov's press office gave several examples, noting that former UK prime minister Rishi Sunak has been engaged by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy as an adviser on economic recovery; former Canadian deputy prime minister and finance minister Chrystia Freeland has become an adviser to Zelenskyy on economic development; and former UK prime minister Boris Johnson has also been involved in international advisory work since leaving government, including in the areas of international policy, security and support for Ukraine.
Fedorov's team said the role of defence innovation adviser is primarily about exchanging management and expert experience in technological warfare, and that this kind of cooperation is important for Ukraine because it "deepens cooperation with NATO countries and their defence industries and creates new opportunities for Ukrainian defence tech companies, joint development projects and investment initiatives".
The press office also noted that Fedorov has dozens of other international cooperation projects planned.
Quote: "At the same time, Mykhailo Fedorov will continue to live and work in Ukraine. His main focus remains here – helping Ukraine defeat the enemy. His international work will enable him to attract more attention, partners and investment to new projects – a think tank and an innovation fund that will invest in Ukrainian technologies and weapons that could change the course of the war."
Background
- On 28 August, Fedorov announced that he had accepted an offer from Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto to become his adviser.
- On 22 August, Fedorov said that following his dismissal from government, his future plans include working on a venture fund to attract investment in Ukrainian defence start-ups, setting up a think tank and civic initiatives aimed at a "return to democracy", and lecturing at universities.

articles.body:

PHOTO Reuters
Font size
Skopje marks the 116th anniversary of Mother Teresa’s birth
“Days of Saint Mother Teresa” are being held in Skopje to mark the 116th anniversary of her birth and the 10th anniversary of her canonization, North Macedonia’s public broadcaster MRT reported. The events began on August 26 with the laying of flowers at a memorial plaque marking the site of the saint’s childhood home in central Skopje and will continue until September 5, the date of her death.
Mother Teresa (Agnes Gonxhe Bojaxhiu) was born on August 26, 1910, in Skopje, to a family of Albanian origin. At the age of 18, she left home and joined the Sisters of Loreto, later moving to India. From 1948 onward, she devoted her life to working among the poorest people of Calcutta. In 1950, she founded the Missionaries of Charity, an order that operates in many countries around the world, providing support to people who are rejected, abandoned, and marginalized. 
In 1979, she received the Nobel Peace Prize for her work helping people in need. She died in Calcutta on September 5, 1997. Pope John Paul II beatified her in 2003, and Pope Francis canonized her on September 4, 2016.
PHOTO Reuters
Former Bosnian Serb commander Ratko Mladić dies in prison
Former commander of the Bosnian Serb Army, General Ratko Mladić, died in prison in The Hague, where he had spent the last 15 years of his life, BNR-Horizont reported, citing Reuters. Several hours earlier, the president of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, Graciela Gatti Santana, had rejected his defense team’s request for early release on humanitarian grounds.
On August 18, Mladić’s defense team requested the release of the 84-year-old and his transfer to a hospital or palliative-care facility in Serbia, citing the likelihood of his death and the need for him to spend more time with his family.
Mladić was sentenced to life imprisonment for genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes committed during the 1992-1995 war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 2021, the Appeals Chamber upheld his sentence, finding him guilty of the genocide of approximately 8,000 Bosniaks in Srebrenica in July 1995, the terrorization of civilians during the siege of Sarajevo, and the taking of UN personnel hostage. Mladić was arrested in Serbia in 2011 and has remained in custody under the supervision of the International Tribunal in The Hague ever since.
PHOTO visitgreece.gr
Drone base to be established on the island of Rhodes
Greece’s Ministry of Defence announced the launch of a procedure to establish a UAV base in the area of a military airfield on the island of Rhodes. This will be Greece’s second such base, following the one on the island of Skyros, BNR correspondent Katya Peeva reported. Until now, drones on Rhodes have been operated from temporary sites, making their use more difficult.
Greece already has a network of companies that design and manufacture their own unmanned aircraft. At the same time, Greece purchases drones from the United States and Israel because domestically produced systems cannot fully meet the needs of the Greek Armed Forces. 
This summer, at special military exercises, Greek manufacturers presented the technologies they are developing, including drones, counter-drone systems, and other types of UAVs. A facility for producing drones using Greek technology is currently under construction near Athens.
PHOTO digi24.ro
Drone fragment containing explosives destroyed on a beach in Romania
A drone fragment containing explosives was discovered on the morning of August 26 near sun loungers on the beach of the Romanian Black Sea resort of Olimp, approximately 38 km south of Constanța. Several people alerted authorities, who immediately cordoned off the area and restricted access for tourists, digi24.ro reported.
Specialists determined that the device contained explosives. It was moved to a hole that had been prepared in the sand and destroyed in a controlled explosion. A warning was sent to local residents and tourists via the RO-Alert system, observatornews.ro reported.
Romanian media reported that a second drone fragment was also discovered, but it posed no threat. The authorities have not provided information about the origin of the device.
PHOTO Pixabay
Average net salary in Croatia reaches €1,555 in June
The average monthly net salary in Croatia rose by 7.7% year-on-year in June 2026, reaching €1,555. In real terms, after accounting for inflation, the increase was 3.1%, the Croatian news agency HINA reported, as cited by BTA. The highest average net salary - €2,330 - was recorded in air transport, while the lowest - €988 -  was in the clothing industry.
The median net salary in June was €1,345, representing a 9.1% increase compared with June 2025.
