articles.title: Royal Navy spent three days tracking Russian vessels in UK waters
articles.body:
The Royal Navy spent three days tracking Russian vessels as they passed through UK waters, it has emerged.
The “intense” 72-hour operation took place last week, with radars used to monitor four ships that made their way from the North Sea through to the Channel.
The fleet was surveilled by HMS Duncan, HMS St Albans and HMS Severn, with a Merlin helicopter providing support, officials said.
The Russian destroyer Admiral Levchenko was observed escorting the cargo vessels General Skobelev and Sparta, which are under sanctions, towards Dover.
In response, Russia deployed its own military resources, including the Neustrashimy frigate, to guard the shipment. Gen Gwyn Jenkins, the First Sea Lord, said there was “no room for complacency” as shadow fleet vessels continued to pose “an unacceptable risk” to UK security.
“Alongside our allies, this approach is forcing Moscow to divert Russian warships away from their core purpose,” he said. “That is because Russia knows we stand ready to act again, should it be required.”
The Royal Navy recently warned of increasing Russian activity in UK waters. In July, it spent 21 days monitoring ships from Moscow, an increase of 25% compared with the previous year. Officials say they have repeatedly observed warships in the Dover strait and the North Sea.
In June, the Royal Marines seized the Russian tanker Smyrtos, the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel, one of more than 500 that have been sanctioned by the UK.
The Kremlin has threatened the UK after Andy Burnham visited Kyiv this week in his first overseas trip as prime minister. During the trip, Burnham said the UK would provide Ukraine with military support, including blueprints for components of long-range Scalp missiles.
Although western officials have tried to play down the prospect of direct conflict between Russia and Nato, the Kremlin has accused the UK and its allies of “playing with fire” in relation to their continued support for Ukraine.
Andrei Fedorov, a former Russian foreign minister, said he could not “100% exclude” the possibility of “semi-military” action against Britain in retaliation, raising the prospect of an attack on British drone factories from “unknown sources”.

articles.title: Iceland's EU referendum sees high preliminary voter turnout in expected close race
articles.body:
In Reykjavík, voter turnout was higher by noon than at the same time during the 2024 parliamentary election, local media reported.
Iceland's capital Reykjavík recorded a higher voter turnout in the high-stakes EU referendum by noon than at the same time during the country's parliamentary elections in 2024, preliminary figures showed on Saturday.
In the hours after voters began casting their ballots in the referendum that will determine whether to reopen EU accession talks, 13.7% had voted by noon in the Reykjavík North constituency, compared to just over 10% in the 2024 election.
In Reykjavík South, just over 14% had voted by noon, compared to just over 11% for the parliamentary election.
More than 20% of voters cast early ballots in advance of election day, Iceland’s national broadcaster RÚV said.
A close race is expected, with a final poll on Friday indicating 50.4% of voters plan to vote yes and 49.6% no.
Backers of EU membership say it’s best for Iceland to get closer to its European neighbours to combat issues that don't respect borders, such as climate change. They also say the euro would bring more stability than Iceland's volatile króna currency.
Opponents say the current setup is just right and that Iceland already enjoys all the benefits of European integration without the sovereignty compromises that inevitably come with full membership. They cite trade deals, such as one with China, that are more favourable.
"I think that we should be a part of a bigger unity. I think it's worth looking into it," Unnur Jokulsdottir, a 71-year-old retiree, said after casting her ballot in Reykjavík's City Hall.
In contrast, Olafur Thorsson, a 53-year-old fish trader, said he was sceptical.
"I used to like the European Union back when it was a good thing. But today it's become a sort of big economic prison," he said.
The country of just under 400,000 people applied to join the EU in the wake of a 2009 financial crisis that devastated its economy.
Membership talks were then suspended in 2013 when a eurosceptic government came to power.
A yes vote would trigger renewed negotiations with the European Commission covering 35 areas, from the economy to human rights.
The issue of fisheries — a pillar of Iceland's economy and over which Reykjavík wants to retain exclusive control — would have to be hammered out with Brussels, which this time around appears more willing to compromise.
On the global stage, the return of war in Europe with Russia's invasion of Ukraine has shaken established security doctrines.
Trump's unpredictability and his threats to take over neighbouring Greenland — which he has mixed up with Iceland on several occasions — have added to Icelanders' concerns.
Their island is strategically located in the sub-Arctic, has no military and depends on NATO and a 1951 bilateral agreement with the United States for its defence.
The result of the vote will be followed closely by the EU, which has not welcomed a wealthy, net contributor to its budget since 1995.

articles.title: German establishment figures call for ban on country’s most popular party
articles.body:
German establishment figures call for ban on country’s most popular party
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Baden-Wurttemberg Governor Cem Ozdemir have called for the opposition Alternative for Germany (AfD) party to be banned. The two establishment politicians claim that the country’s most popular party poses a threat to Germany’s constitutional order and democracy.
The AfD is the largest opposition force in the Bundestag and enjoys the support of 28% of respondents, according to recent surveys.
The right-wing party advocates tougher immigration controls while also calling for an end to Germany’s green policies. It is also highly critical of Berlin’s support for Ukraine and sanctions against Russia.
In an opinion piece published by the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung on Friday, Pistorius and Ozdemir drew parallels between the modern-day AfD and Adolf Hitler’s National Socialist party.
“Today, we are once again facing a threat to democracy from the extreme right,” the politicians, who represent the Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the Green Party, respectively, claimed.
In making their case for outlawing the right-wing party, Pistorius and Ozdemir argued that a powerful faction within the AfD espouses the idea of ‘remigration’, thus calling into question the “inviolability of human dignity” enshrined in the German constitution.
“We cannot confront ethnic nationalist ideology through political debate. That would be naive,” the authors wrote.
“A legal review of the constitutionality of a political party is warranted when it calls into question and threatens the continued existence of our democracy,” Pistorius and Ozdemir stated.
The two also took issue with the AfD’s supposedly “pro-Russian stance,” describing it as a “security risk.” The opposition party’s calls for Germany to withdraw from the European Union, the Eurozone, and NATO are equally “dangerous,” according to the article.
While acknowledging the AfD’s rising popularity, Pistorius and Ozdemir argued that widespread public support for the party is another reason why it should be banned outright.
Voting for the opposition party out of dissatisfaction with the current state of affairs in Germany is no excuse, the authors argued.
“The undeniable radicalization of the AfD makes it impossible to claim ignorance of who one is voting for,” they wrote.
At present, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency classifies the AfD as a ‘suspected right-wing extremist’ entity – a designation that gives the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV) powers to surveil the party and its members. In several regions, local AfD chapters have been subjected to even wider monitoring.
Meanwhile, an INSA poll published by Bild earlier this month showed that support for Germany’s governing Christian Democratic CDU/CSU bloc had fallen to 20%, with some 78% of respondents dissatisfied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s coalition government, which also includes the Social Democrats.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Blasts 'Negligence' As Ukraine Mourns Dozens Killed In Russian Strike
articles.body:
KYIV -- Ukrainian crews early on August 30 continued to search for victims of the deadly Russian attack outside of Kyiv, while local residents -- as well as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy -- demanded answers as to why explosives were stored in a warehouse so near private housing.
"A terrible situation and terrible negligence on the part of those who stored explosives right next to people," Zelenskyy said late on August 29 in his nightly video address.
"There has been extensive destruction, and as of now, 37 people have been reported killed. The rubble is still being cleared, and unfortunately, the death toll may increase."
Zelenskyy said the Russian drone strike was on an ammunition storage site "that definitely shouldn’t have been there...shells, mines, other ammunition, and drones detonated."
He added that a criminal investigation was under way.
"All the facts must be fully investigated. Another such crime -- after what happened in Vyshneve -- is absolutely unacceptable. I expect the details to be presented to the public promptly," he said.
In July, a similar incident occurred in the Vyshneve region of Kyiv where a Russian strike caused explosions at a warehouse, killing nine people and damaging more than 280 houses.
Explosive Storage
Following the latest attack, Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky also criticized officials for storing explosive materials near residential areas. He said making such mistakes was "criminal negligence.”
Along with the fatalities, dozens of people were injured from the overnight Russian drone strike on Ukraine’s Bucha district in the Kyiv region.
Local authorities said the August 28 drone strike caused a major fire and explosions at the warehouse, which is said to be the major cause of the casualties.
Reporting from the scene, RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service correspondent Maryan Kushnir said that “the whole area is in ruins,” adding that the strike also affected a nursing home, where “many” people were killed.
According to Tymur Tkachenko, a top district administration official, those killed in Bucha also included the head of the Dmytrivka community in the district, Taras Didych. Tkachenko said it was a “great loss” for the region.
Operational HQ
The official added that an operational headquarters had been set up in Dmytrivka to provide food as well as other support to the people in the affected region.
As sounds of detonations continued in Myla village, local resident Zhanna told RFE/RL that she had lost her husband in the incident, adding that he had previously survived the Russian occupation.
“Why can’t this be organized?” she asked through tears, referring to the placement of explosives in the village.
Another Myla local, Oleksandr, said the village’s residents didn’t know what was stored in the warehouse there. “Nobody told us anything... People aren’t informed. I think everything is being done the wrong way.”

articles.title: Estonian FM calls for increased pressure on Russia following overnight attack on Ukraine
articles.body:
Estonian FM calls for increased pressure on Russia following overnight attack on Ukraine
According to Ukrinform, the Estonian foreign minister stated this on the social media platform X.
"Another night of Russian drone barrages tore across Ukraine, with the village of Myla absorbing one of the heaviest strikes. Russian drones shredded critical infrastructure, hit warehouses, residential blocks, care homes, and killed 27 people," Tsahkna said.
He added that Odesa, Dnipro and Kyiv were also targeted by Russian attacks overnight.
"Russia's objective is clear: terror and destruction. This week's repeated strikes on critical infrastructure show a calculated effort to leave Ukrainians cold, hungry and in the dark before winter. Kremlin's plan must fail," the Estonian diplomat emphasized.
Tsahkna stressed that support for Ukraine must remain unwavering and sustained across all areas.
"Pressure on Russia must intensify, stronger sanctions, deeper international isolation, zero concessions," Tsahkna urged.
As Ukrinform reported, 27 people were killed and more than 40 injured in a Russian attack in Kyiv region's Bucha district on the evening of August 28.
In Kyiv region's Boryspil district, a 14-year-old girl was killed in a Russian drone attack on the morning of August 29. There were also other casualties.
Sunday, August 30, has been declared a day of mourning in Kyiv region for the victims of the Russian attack.

articles.title: Iran's economy strains as war, US sanctions intensify
articles.body:
Iranian leaders are increasingly acknowledging the economic toll of the war with the United States, with the supreme leader urging the government to address growing hardships and President Masoud Pezeshkian saying foreign trade has fallen by a third because of U.S. sanctions and a blockade.
Yet Tehran showed no sign of backing down Saturday, vowing to withstand U.S. pressure, pursue diplomacy and maintain what it described as control over the Strait of Hormuz.
The strategic waterway gives Iran significant leverage because any disruption there could affect global energy markets.
The government said in a statement carried by state media that easing economic pressures caused by sanctions and war remained a central priority. Its measures include curbing inflation, stabilizing markets, creating jobs, directing investment toward domestic production and gradually reducing the country's reliance on the dollar.
Six months after the United States and Israel launched the war, negotiations remain deadlocked, while President Donald Trump's administration has intensified efforts to squeeze Iran financially through what it has described as an "economic D-Day."
Washington has warned countries to cut business ties with Iran or face secondary sanctions, though the Treasury Department stopped short of imposing penalties against major Iranian trade partners such as China and India, which could have repercussions for the U.S. and global economies.
The Treasury imposed sanctions on Egypt's Banque Misr for doing business with Tehran, proposing a rule that would cut off the bank's branches in the United Arab Emirates from dollar transactions.
Egypt's central bank said it and the foreign ministry were in contact with U.S. officials regarding the matter, adding that the measure was limited to Banque Misr's UAE branch and its U.S. dollar transactions with correspondent banks.
Banque Misr later said in a statement that it was reviewing the U.S. Treasury notice, adding that its branch in the UAE continued to provide banking services to customers in line with applicable rules and procedures.
The U.S. also imposed sanctions on an entity based in Hong Kong and a person linked to Iran's Bank Melli, according to a notice posted on the Treasury's website.
The sanctions drive is compounding the toll of the war on Iran's economy, where annual inflation reached 66% last month.
Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen publicly since he was injured in the initial Feb. 28 attack that killed his father and predecessor, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, called on the government to tackle the economic hardship.
"There is the need to seriously address the chain of economic and livelihood challenges, such as inflation, unemployment, management of prices and the market for goods and services," according to a written statement attributed to Khamenei.
President Masoud Pezeshkian told state media that Iranian exports and imports had slumped nearly 35% because of U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade of Iranian ports.
But he said Iran was able to sell about 90 million barrels of oil during the short-lived memorandum of understanding that the U.S. and Iran signed in June, when Washington permitted Iranian oil sales.
With the U.S. focused on its economic pressure campaign, others have sought to revive diplomatic efforts to end the war.
Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani met with Iranian leaders in Tehran on Thursday. He said he had stressed during the meeting the importance of returning to the prewar status of open shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi on Friday described the talks with Al Thani as "creative."
In Saturday's statement, Iran said diplomacy and defense were "two complementary, coordinated and inseparable wings" for protecting the country's national interests, security and territorial integrity. It said it would pursue both tracks in a balanced manner.
Qatar, a U.S. ally and Gulf neighbor to Iran, and Pakistan helped broker the June memorandum of understanding that led to a brief ceasefire before disagreements over the vital strait caused it to unravel. Before the war, the waterway carried 20% of the world's oil and LNG.
U.S. military commanders say American forces have cleared sea mines from the strait that had been laid months ago by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Trump has repeatedly said the Strait of Hormuz is open, but the Revolutionary Guards' navy said in a statement that such claims "are an obvious lie," reiterating that the waterway remained closed to ships without Iranian permission.
Only seven commodity vessels transited the strait on Thursday, down from 17 a day earlier and below the 10-day average of 15, preliminary shipping data showed Friday.

articles.title: Polish premier says next 6 months decisive as Russian escalation grows
articles.body:
Jo Harper
29 August 2026•Update: 29 August 2026
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Saturday that Russian escalation was continuing and warned that the next six months could be decisive for European security, following talks with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte.
Tusk said Rutte had briefed him on the situation in the region and on the Ukrainian-Russian front, adding that Ukraine required greater air support and that European NATO members needed to prepare for different scenarios.
“As I warned, escalation on Russia’s part is progressing,” Tusk wrote on X. “Ukraine needs greater support in the air, which is also important for our security. This is a task for all of Europe.”
“The next six months will be decisive,” he added, saying Poland and other NATO countries must be prepared for a range of possible developments.
“We cannot rule out a provocation by Russia against one of the NATO members,” Tusk said.
The comments deepen warnings Tusk issued on Friday, when he said the war had reached a turning point and that Russia appeared to be preparing to escalate tensions both in Ukraine and across the wider region.
Tusk said then that Poland had been receiving information from US intelligence and was aware of discussions surrounding an unusual visit to Moscow this week by CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
“We must be prepared for different eventualities,” Tusk said Friday, describing the coming months as “critical.” He also referred to an earlier warning that Russia could attempt a limited attack against a NATO country.
Ratcliffe's Moscow visit has drawn heightened attention after reports that the CIA chief raised concerns with Russian officials about possible military action against NATO territory. 
The Kremlin rejected reports that the visit was intended to warn Moscow against such an attack.
US President Donald Trump on Thursday played down those concerns, saying he did not believe Russian President Vladimir Putin would attack a NATO member and describing Ratcliffe's meeting with his Russian counterpart as routine.
Tusk's latest remarks also come as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine and European governments debate how to strengthen Kyiv's air defences while maintaining their own military readiness.

articles.title: EU enters ‘winter panic’ mode as gas storage hits record low – Guardian
articles.body:
EU enters ‘winter panic’ mode as gas storage hits record low – Guardian
EU gas storage is now at one of the lowest seasonal levels on record, with the shortfall feeding a “winter panic” among traders amid the Iran war and Brussels’s continued push to phase out Russian energy, according to The Guardian.
EU gas stocks are at around 64% as of Friday, far below the 80% average maintained during this season over the past several years, according to the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG).
For comparison, EU stocks were at about 66% on August 29, 2021, and around 72% on the same date in 2013, although the fill level typically drops much lower in winter months when consumption is high.
As for the country breakdown, German gas storage is only slightly above 50% capacity, while the Netherlands is at around 45% and Belgium around 50%, according to recent GIE readings.
Officials in the Netherlands in particular have complained that they expect to miss their planned winter targets, and are blaming sluggish injections and poor commercial incentives for traders to buy gas now and store it for winter.
Meanwhile, the UK’s facilities are only at around 30% capacity, although the country has historically relied more on continuous imports than storage.
Amid the crunch, natural gas prices have risen above €66 ($76) per megawatt-hour, more than double from levels earlier in the year, according to the Trading Economics website.
Speaking to The Guardian, Bjarne Schieldrop, chief commodities analyst at SEB, remarked that the market had “stayed relatively calm” this summer, hoping that the traffic through the Strait of Hormuz will normalize.
However, now “no one expects it to happen any time soon,” he said, adding: “As a result, the European natural gas market has run into a bit of a winter panic over the past week.”
The weak storage position leaves the market more exposed to cold weather, low wind generation and unforeseen supply disruptions. Gas analyst Greg Molnar told the paper that “low storage levels are naturally increasing the risk of heightened winter price volatility.”
The immediate pressure comes from the de facto closure of the Strait of Hormuz that disrupted Qatari LNG exports. While Qatar supplied only 6.6% of LNG to the EU in the first quarter of 2026 – compared to the 57% supplied by the US – the Middle East conflict has intensified competition between European and Asian buyers for energy, prompting a rally in gas prices.
The shortfall also comes as the EU maintains sweeping sanctions on Moscow and has vowed to wean itself of Russian energy. While Russia provided around 45% of EU gas imports in 2021, its share had dropped to only about 12% by 2025.
After the EU imposed sweeping sanctions on Russia in 2022, it endured one of the worst energy crises in decades. Gas prices exploded to more than €300 per megawatt-hour, hitting industry and consumers alike, with EU countries reeling from soaring inflation and costs of living.
When the EU began cutting its dependence on oil and gas from Russia following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova suggested that the bloc was on a “suicidal” course and was “shooting itself in the head.”

articles.title: Russia still aims to create 'buffer zone' in northern Ukraine – Ukrainian President Office official
articles.body:
Russia’s plans to create a buffer zone in Kharkiv, Sumy and, partially, Chernihiv regions remain unchanged – to a depth of up to 20 kilometers, with the possibility of further expansion, Deputy Head of Ukraine’s Office of the President Pavlo Palisa said.
As an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent reported, he said this during a meeting with journalists.
"The previous plans to create a buffer zone in Kharkiv and Sumy regions, and partially in Chernihiv region, to a depth of up to 20 kilometers and with the possibility of further expansion also remain in place. The expansion of this buffer zone is primarily linked to changes in the technical and tactical-technical characteristics of unmanned aerial vehicles," he explained.
The brigadier general noted that "figuratively speaking, the kill zone is growing, and the capabilities of drones are growing."
Commenting on reports about the possible opening of new fronts, he confirmed that the Ukrainian side had indeed received intelligence information, verified through several sources, that the military leadership of the Russian Armed Forces had received an assignment from the political leadership to plan such an operation under several scenarios toward Kyiv and Chernihiv.
"I ask you to pay attention to this: plan and prepare. So, indeed, several options were being considered there. Accordingly, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has developed possible options for responding to, defending against, protecting against and countering these actions," he said.
According to Palisa, Ukraine does not currently see the creation of an offensive grouping in these directions. He stressed that the priority task for the Ukrainian side is "to prevent conditions from being created that would allow the Russians to launch any offensive actions at all."

articles.title: Turkiye summons Ukraine ambassador over Black Sea attacks
articles.body:
Turkiye summons Ukraine ambassador over Black Sea attacks
Two Turkish-operated vessels have been struck this week as a result of the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Ukraine’s ambassador to Turkiye has been summoned to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Ankara following two attacks on Turkish-operated vessels in the Black Sea.
Turkish officials communicated their concerns to Ambassador Naryman Dzhelialo at the ministry on Saturday, the AFP news agency reported.

“During the meeting, Turkiye warned about the absolute need to ensure the safety of people, of assets, of navigation and of the environment in the Black Sea,” the ministry said in a statement.
The meeting comes after the Turkish-operated container ship Lider Bordo Mavi was struck in the Black Sea on Wednesday, when it was off the coast of Tuapse, Russia.
The Lider Kocatepe was also targeted by a drone when on its way to assist the Lider Bordo Mavi the next day. Turkish media reported that the Lider Bordo Mavi was towed to the Turkish port of Samsun.
Turkiye has been calling for a halt to attacks on civilian vessels in the Black Sea as Ukraine and Russia continue to target each other’s export revenues. Navigating the sea has carried heightened risk ever since Russia launched its war on Ukraine in February 2022, but attacks there have escalated.
Several commercial Turkish ships have been hit by drones thought to have been launched by Ukraine. Three crew members were seriously injured when the Nadezhda cargo ship was hit by a drone near the Russian port of Novorossiysk earlier this month.
Turkiye maintains relations with both Moscow and Kyiv, and has positioned itself as a mediator between the two sides. It has not applied Western sanctions on Russia, and has sold US-made defence equipment to Ukraine. A free trade agreement between Turkiye and Ukraine was ratified by the Ukrainian government in July.
However, the issue of safety in the Black Sea is crucial for Turkiye, as its commercial vessels regularly transit the waterway.
Earlier this month, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan called for a halt to attacks in the Black Sea, saying, “They are attacking all commercial shipping without distinction.”

articles.title: India news: PM Modi in Uzbekistan on way to SCO summit
articles.body:
India news: PM Modi in Uzbekistan on way to SCO summit
Published August 29, 2026last updated August 29, 2026
What you need to know
- Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has arrived in Uzbekistan for bilateral talks
- Hundreds of Indians remain missing in Nepal floods
- Indian opposition claims Sonia Gandhi's memoir dropped by Penguin India over Modi, RSS and China
- Controversial Hindu nationalist group chief Mohan Bhagwat set to deliver speech in NYC
Here are the biggest headlines from India on Saturday, August 29, and Sunday, August 30.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.
We're pausing our coverage
We're pausing our India news coverage for Saturday.
Stay tuned for more on Sunday in this blog with DW!
Modi lands in Uzbekistan en route to Russia-Asia summit
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi posted pictures of himself and Uzbekistan's President Shavkat Mirziyoyev to social media on Saturday, thanking his political counterpart for the warm welcome and writing on X: "Landed in Tashkent to a warm welcome by President Shavkat Mirziyoyev. Grateful to him for the special gesture."
Modi went on to emphasize, "This is my fourth visit to Uzbekistan, reflecting the depth and growing momentum of our bilateral relations."
Modi is scheduled to attend dinner with Mirziyoyev on Saturday.
The two will hold bilateral meetings on Sunday before departing for the Kyrgyz Republic and the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit.
Modi is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin during the Kyrgyz summit.
Kolkata Police file First Information Report against former West Bengal Chief Minister Banerjee
Kolkata Police on Saturday registered a First Information Report (FIR) against former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee for allegedly violating a Calcutta High Court order on a students' wing rally held on Friday.
A FIR is written document informing police of a crime and gives the authorities necessary information to launch an investigation.
Several Indian media outlets reported on the FIR. A Hindustan Times report said that the city's high court had permitted Banerjee to celebrate the foundation day of her party's youth wing on Cathedral Road in central Kolkata but had directed that one side of the road be kept operational.
Local police said that the flank was not left open and the court-specified time-limit was exceeded.
The FIR was filed against Banerjee and organizers of the rally, officers quoted by news agency Press Trust of India said.
"The FIR has been registered for the alleged violation of the court's order. The role of all those involved in the violation will be examined during the course of the investigation," the officer said.
The police also claimed the student wing supporters "breached barricades and jostled with police personnel deployed for maintaining law and order," PTI reported.
Banerjee is the leader of the Trinamool Congress Party, a major regional party in the eastern state of West Bengal. She is the former chief minister of the state and was unseated earlier this year by Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party — after 15 years in power.
Incidentally, at the rally, Banerjee had claimed that the police had turned into a "monstrous entity" under BJP rule and pledged to stop "police atrocities" on her supporters.
WATCH — Basmati rice: India, Pakistan and the EU dispute
The fight over basmati rice has become one of the most complex disputes in the global food trade.
Both India and Pakistan claim the premium, aromatic rice as part of their agriculture and cultural heritage, and both are seeking European Union recognition for its geographical origin.
But years after the first application was filed in 2018, the EU has yet to decide how the name should be protected and by whom.
Basmati is among the world's most valuable rice varieties, generating significant export revenues and carrying strong historical ties to the Punjab region, which spans both countries.
Meanwhile, experts warn that widespread misuse of the name on international markets could undermine future protection altogether. As Brussels weighs its options, the outcome could have far-reaching consequences.
Congress slams Penguin India for backing out of Sonia Gandhi's memoir
Leaders of India's largest opposition party, the Indian National Congress (INC), alleged that publishing house Penguin India was pressured to back out of publishing veteran politician Sonia Gandhi's memoir due to portions related to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a Hindu nationalist group, and China's alleged occupation of Indian territory under Modi's rule.
Sonia Gandhi has been a leading figure in Indian politics for decades. She was the president of the INC from 1998 to 2017 and is the party's longest-serving chief.
Earlier this month, Alfred A. Knopf announced that Gandhi's "Belonging: A Journey of Love" will be published on November 10. Knopf is a publishing imprint under Penguin Random House.
"Suppressing the book of Sonia Gandhi, a person of such stature, a senior leader of the nation, and former Leader of the Opposition, under pressure is tantamount to the murder of freedom of Expression," senior INC leader Ashok gehlot said in a post on X.
"The real issue is that pressure was put on Penguin India to remove the portions related to Modi, the RSS, and the occupation of Indian territory by China during Modi's rule. This is the murder of democracy," he said.
In another post, Gehlot said "there's some kind of pressure. It could be from the PMO [Prime Minister's Office] or someone else — that time will tell."
This comes a day after Penguin India released a statement of clarification: "Any suggestion that Penguin Random House India decided not to publish 'Belonging' because the author declined editorial changes does not accurately reflect the circumstances."
The statement was referring to a report by The Indian Express which said the publishing house would not publish the book in India because "editorial changes and deletions" were turned down by the author.
"As a publisher, it is both our prerogative and our responsibility to fact check and provide authors with recommendations that are in best interests of their books," Penguin India said in its statement, adding that it "remained willing and keen to publish the book."
India monitors glaciers after Nepal disaster
Days after deadly flash floods triggered by a glacial collapse swept through the Tibet-Nepal border, India stepped up monitoring of the glaciers in its Himalayan region bordering Nepal and China.
Although the exact cause of the collapse remains unclear, global warming has increased the likelihood of such disasters.
"Since we share a border with Nepal, as a neighbor, and also have a similar geographic situation... we have asked our department to monitor all the glaciers and known glacial lakes in the region," said Madan Kaushik, state disaster management minister in India's Himalayan state of Uttarakhand.
"We have asked our teams to be vigilant and monitor if a similar situation is emerging anywhere in the state," he added.
Kaushik's state is one of India's most ecologically sensitive regions with over 1,266 glacial lakes.
Indian Hindu nationalist group's chief set to address thousands in NYC
Mohan Bhagwat, the chief of a controversial right-wing Hindu nationalist group in India closely associated with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, is set to address about 5,000 members of Indian American groups in New York City on Saturday.
The event titled "Universal Oneness Celebration" is being held at the Infosys Theater in Madison Square Garden and is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue.
It is being met with protests, a denunciation from the city's mayor Zohran Mamdani and a call for sanctions by a US panel on religious freedom.
Bhagwat's link with Modi
Bhagwat is the chief of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for "National Volunteer Organization."
The group describes itself as a "Hindu-centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus. It disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance.
The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization.
Why is the RSS controversial?
In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities.
However, several interfaith and civil rights groups — including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York — have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history.
The US Commission on International Religious Freedom (USCIRF), a government advisory body, has called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims."
Recently, it called for the US government to impose targeted sanctions on RSS members, including Bhagwat, and Indian officials who support the group.
The Ministry of External Affairs in India quickly rejected the commission’s remarks, calling the body biased and lacking in credibility.
United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more.
WATCH: Nepal village buried in mud
DW correspondent Adil Bhat reports from a village in Nepal's Nuwakot district that was buried in mud after severe flooding.
Over 300 Indians still missing in Nepal-Tibet floods
At least 320 Indian nationals were still unaccounted for in the Nepal-Tibet floods as of Friday evening, according to the latest update from India's foreign ministry.
A glacier collapse on Wednesday unleashed a huge torrentof rock, ice, mud and debris through Himalayan mountain river systems, killing more than 600 people in Nepal and China's Tibet. Over 2,000 people are missing.
Here's the latest update on Indian nationals:
- 84 Indian nationals have been rescued so far, including 21 from Tamil Nadu who have returned to India and 63 who were working at the Trishuli-I power project in Nepal
- 149 crossed over into Nepal from China
- Around 400 are safe in China, the Indian Embassy in Beijing is working on their evacuation
- 320 are missing or unreachable
Meanwhile, India dispatched a third flight carrying relief supplies to Nepal on Friday evening. The flight also carried an 11-member medical and tunnel rescue team, who are now working on the ground, according to India's Foreign Minister, Subrahmanyam Jaishankar.
Modi is en route to Uzbekistan for bilateral talks
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi left for a state visit to Uzbekistan, where he is set to discuss ways of deepening cooperation with President Shavkat Mirziyoyev.
Ahead of departure, Modi said he looked forward to his discussions with the Uzbek president to "further deepening our cooperation in trade and investment, digital connectivity, defence, energy, and on advancing our shared visions of Viksit Bharat and Yangi Uzbekistan."
"Viksit Bharat" roughly translates to "Developed India" and is a commonly used term by Modi and his ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. "Yangi Uzbekistan" translates to "New Uzbekistan" and is a political slogan used by Mirziyoyev.
On Saturday, Modi will attend a dinner hosted by Mirziyoyev, followed by bilateral engagements with him on Sunday at the Presidential Palace.
After his two-day state visit to Uzbekistan, Modi will travel to the Kyrgyz Republic to attend the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit, where he is also scheduled to hold a bilateral meeting with the Russian President, Vladimir Putin.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello and welcome to DW's India blog!
This is Mahima Kapoor reporting from the Delhi studio and I will be your guide through the chaotic news cycle of the world's most populous nation.
Hundreds of Indians remain missing in the devastating Nepal-Tibet flash floods, as of the Indian foreign ministry's last update. Most of those unaccounted for or stranded were either working in Nepal or were pilgrims visiting the Kailash Mansarovar site in China's Tibet.
Indian embassies in Kathmandu and Beijing are working closely with local authorities, and Delhi has sent at least three tranches of aid.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi embarked on a four-day official trip to Central Asia. He will first visit Uzbekistan to hold bilateral discussions and further cooperation between the two nations. Modi will then attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Kyrgyzstan for the last two days of his tour.
Stay tuned for all of this and more!

articles.title: Russia could have used nukes in Ukraine but chose restraint – top MP
articles.body:
Russia could have used nukes in Ukraine but chose restraint – top MP
Russia could have long ago used tactical nuclear weaponry to achieve victory against Ukraine, but it has always sought to minimize collateral damage, Leonid Slutsky, the head of Russia’s Liberal-Democratic Party (LDPR), has said.
The senior MP, who chairs the Russian State Duma International Affairs Committee, made the remarks in an interview with conservative American journalist and podcaster Tucker Carlson that aired on Saturday. Slutsky said Moscow would only opt for nuclear weaponry against Kiev if its Western sponsors supplied Ukraine with weapons of mass destruction. The politician expressed hope that the situation would not deteriorate to that point.
In any other scenario, use of nuclear weaponry against Ukraine would not fit Moscow’s approach and vision, the MP stated.
“We could have used them long ago and achieved victory, but we always rely on common sense and the principle of minimizing civilian casualties. Using such weapons as an instrument of terror, as was the case in Hiroshima and Nagasaki, if we recall World War II, is alien to us,” Slutsky stated.
Moscow could also have begun hitting Ukraine without any regard for collateral damage and civilian casualties, but still hopes that Kiev and its Western backers will show some “common sense” and come to the “position of peace, not war,” the politician believes.
“But for now they take an entirely different position, completely devoid of common sense,” Slutsky said.
Russia has so far avoided attacking bridges across the Dnieper River, the destruction of which would have deprived the Ukrainian military in Donbass of logistics, the politician explained. He said it has also refrained from striking the key airport of Borispol outside Kiev, which has been used to funnel weaponry from the West. Either option, however, would have drastically worsened the humanitarian situation in Ukraine and harmed civilians, according to Slutsky.

articles.title: Most of those killed by explosions in Bucha were elderly care home residents – photos
articles.body:
Most of those killed by explosions in Bucha were elderly care home residents – photos
Most of the 37 people killed as a result of a Russian UAV strike and the subsequent detonation of ammunition in the village of Myla, in the Bucha district near Kyiv, were residents of a care home for the elderly.
Source: hromadske, citing Svitlana Vodolaha, a spokesperson for Ukraine's State Emergency Service, and its own correspondents; hromadske journalist Diana Butsko on Facebook
Details: Vodolaha said the deaths of 27 people have so far been confirmed. The other 10 cases have not been confirmed, as these relate to human remains found at the site of the Russian attack. The exact number of people killed will only be known after they have been identified.
According to hromadske's correspondents, the private care home for the elderly was the worst affected, and most of the people killed were residents of the home. The State Emergency Service said at least 27 residents were killed.
The spokesperson for the State Emergency Service also said that "literally within the first few seconds" after first responders arrived, they rescued 10 people who were outside or trapped in basements and unable to get out on their own. Overall, firefighters and police officers evacuated around 400 people that night.
The State Emergency Service also said that firefighters from other regions have been brought in to deal with the aftermath of the attack. It is currently unclear when the work will be completed, as it is being hampered by further Russian attacks.
Butsko said on Facebook that the care home was called Dobryi Dim (Good Home).
"Everyone who was in the building was killed. At least 31 bodies have been found. Three people from the local area were also killed. Two died in the building opposite the care home, and one person was in a car," she reported.
According to Butsko, local residents heard two strikes, the first at 20:30 on 28 August. The explosions continued throughout the night.
Background:
- Powerful explosions were heard in the Bucha district of Kyiv Oblast on the evening of 28 August. A warehouse facility caught fire, and all traffic was blocked in both directions on the M-06 Kyiv-Chop road between kilometres 15 and 32.
- As of 29 August, local authorities reported that the death toll from the Russian attack and subsequent detonation in the Bucha district has risen to 37, while another 42 people were injured.
- Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has stated that ammunition cannot be stored near residential buildings. He also said the first strike in Myla village hit a defence forces warehouse that "should not have been there".
- Commenting on the deaths of dozens of people after the Russian strike on Myla, Ukraine's General Staff said Russia is the root cause of the tragedy.
- The Security Service of Ukraine has launched a criminal investigation into the Russian strike on warehouses in the Bucha district.

articles.title: Israel launches airstrikes, drone attacks on south Lebanon
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel launches airstrikes, drone attacks on south Lebanon
The Israeli army launched a series of airstrikes and drone attacks on southern Lebanon on Saturday, while attacking several towns with artillery. Israeli forces also set fire to homes and wooded areas in border areas. 
Among the towns targeted weere Nabatieh al-Fawqa, Mansouri, Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh, and Qaaqaiyet al-Jisr.
Lebanon’s official National News Agency (NNA) said that Israeli warplanes carried out a series of airstrikes on Saturday afternoon targeting the area between Al-Deir and the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge, north of Nabatieh al-Fawqa. 
The strikes came after the town was targeted twice by drones during the morning. An Israeli drone carried out a strike at around 8:55 am local time, before another drone struck the town for a second time.
Israeli warplanes also struck the town of Mansouri in two separate waves, and later in the afternoon targeted the valley between the towns of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh and Qaaqaiyet al-Jisr in Nabatieh Governorate. Around the same time, Israeli artillery shelled the town of Haris.
In another attack, the Israeli army began setting fires in the area between Aita al-Jabal and Haddatha in the morning. 
Strong winds caused the fires to spread, consuming areas of woodland and vegetation. Firefighting teams have faced difficulties reaching the area and extinguishing the blazes.
NNA also reported that Israeli occupation forces set fire to homes in the town of Beit Yahoun. No immediate information was available regarding the extent of the damage caused by the attack.

articles.title: IDF warns budget freeze is pushing military readiness ‘to the edge’
articles.body:
Senior Israeli defense officials are warning that a deepening budget dispute with the Finance Ministry is beginning to threaten the military’s operational readiness, with promised funding still undelivered, shortages emerging in key equipment and major procurement deals already falling through.
“The Budget Department has put on the brakes completely and we are on the edge of an abyss,” a senior defense official said in closed-door discussions, describing what the military sees as an increasingly serious threat to its ability to sustain operations over the long term.
The warning follows IDF Chief of Staff Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir’s statement last week that “the coffers are empty,” as tensions between the military and Finance Ministry intensify.
Defense officials say the government and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu acknowledged a NIS 40 billion ($13.4 billion) budget gap and directed that NIS 15 billion ($5.03 billion) be transferred immediately. According to the military, that money has still not arrived.
The dispute comes as Israel continues military operations on multiple fronts, including Iran, Lebanon, Gaza, the West Bank and the Syrian border.
Officials say the funding shortage is already affecting routine maintenance and efforts to rebuild capabilities depleted during prolonged fighting.
Hundreds of IDF Humvees were destroyed during combat in Lebanon, according to the defense establishment, creating what officials describe as a severe shortage. The problem could become more difficult to resolve because production in the United States of Humvees configured for Israeli use is expected to end soon.
Domestic production lines for some ground-force munitions are also nearing the end of their current orders, officials said. Without new contracts, manufacturers could halt production, while defense companies such as Elbit Systems and Rafael cannot be expected to finance continued production themselves.
Apache deal expires
The budget dispute has also affected Israeli efforts to strengthen the Air Force.
A planned purchase of Apache attack helicopters from the United States, developed over the past two years, has formally expired after failing to reach the political leadership for approval.
Defense planners had considered the helicopters important for border defense and ongoing combat operations.
“After the Americans submitted a formal framework, the Budget Department dug in its heels to prevent the deal from reaching the political echelon for approval, and after several extensions requested by the Defense Ministry and the IDF, the deal officially expired,” the senior defense official said.
The official warned that losing major procurement opportunities could have consequences beyond the immediate equipment shortfall.
“Every missed deal like this harms relations with the U.S. administration, raises prices in the global market, especially when countries in the region, such as Qatar, buy platforms like refueling aircraft at enormous prices and drive up the cost, and above all creates a serious operational gap on the ground.”
Defense officials reject Finance Ministry arguments that the military receives effectively unlimited funding without sufficient oversight.
They point to several layers of financial supervision, including approval by the accountant general, Finance Ministry representatives inside the Defense Ministry and a dedicated comptroller in the military budget directorate.
The IDF also notes that it received praise from the State Comptroller for efficiency measures.
Military says spending demands reflect expanding war
Defense officials say the original budget imposed on the IDF was NIS 111 billion ($37.25 billion), well below the NIS 143 billion ($47.99 billion) the military had requested, while planned reserve-duty days were also reduced.
The defense budget was later increased to NIS 143 billion ($47.99 billion), but officials say the gap between actual funding and the requirements generated by government-directed operations subsequently widened to NIS 40 billion ($13.4 billion).
They attribute the increase to the expansion of military activity, including a deep ground operation in Lebanon, a 40-day campaign against Iran, control over 62% of the Gaza Strip, maintenance of a security zone in Syria and intensified operations in the West Bank and along Israel’s eastern border, including efforts to counter drone threats.
The military is particularly concerned that the dispute could extend into an election period and leave Israel without an approved state budget until summer 2027.
Defense officials say even senior government legal advisers have accepted that some of the military’s immediate requests, particularly replenishing stockpiles and preventing production lines from shutting down, are urgent operational requirements rather than political spending.
Ammunition, spare parts for naval and ground platforms and border-defense systems are among the needs the military describes as entirely nonpolitical.
“The NIS 15 billion ($5.03 billion) that has already been agreed upon must be transferred immediately, and the budget must be reopened in the government to create a planning horizon,” defense officials said.
“The price that is not paid today in money will be paid tomorrow in national security.”

articles.title: Germany's Merz plans to blame Russia for drone incident in Leipzig
articles.body:
Germany's Merz plans to blame Russia for drone incident in Leipzig
Politico has learned that German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is preparing to hold Russia responsible for a recent attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport and respond with sanctions.
Source: Politico, a Brussels-based politics and policy news organisation, citing its sources, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Politico notes that Merz plans to blame Russia for the appearance of a drone fitted with explosives at Leipzig airport and respond with sanctions, in parallel with the EU's preparations for its next sanctions package.
The announcement is reportedly planned for the beginning of next week to coincide with a meeting of the EU Foreign Affairs Council in Ireland, although it could come earlier if the chancellor decides.
Two of the sources cited by Politico compared Berlin's upcoming announcements to Zeitenwende 2.0 – the major change in Germany's defence policy announced by former Chancellor Olaf Scholz in response to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
According to one source, the German government believes that expelling individual Russian diplomats or closing the Russian House Russian Houses are cultural centres established in other countries to promote Russia's language and culture and Russian education. They also serve as platforms for Russian state propaganda and soft power in Berlin would no longer be an adequate response to the Leipzig drone incident. Berlin believes the response should involve significantly tougher sanctions or further increases in military assistance to Ukraine.
Merz said on 25 August that there would be serious consequences for the incident in Leipzig, but he did not name those responsible.
In response to an official request for comment on these plans, the German government said it "does not engage in speculation".
"The only thing that matters is the official attribution made by the federal government at its own discretion and after weighing all the results of the investigation," the spokesperson said.
Background:
- On 4 August, a drone fitted with explosives was discovered at Leipzig/Halle airport near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft that was being used to transport military equipment.
- According to media reports, the German security authorities have almost no doubt that Moscow was behind the incident.
- US intelligence has linked the incident to Russia. The Russian Embassy in Berlin called the Leipzig incident a fabricated provocation.

articles.title: Trump Promises His Venezuela Oil Deal Will Lower Gas Prices. But When?
articles.body:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that the United States has entered a “historic” deal with Venezuela, saying that it gives the U.S. majority control over more than 65 billion barrels of oil reserves. Calling it the “BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY” in a post on Truth Social, he said that the agreement would “substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans.”
The Trump Administration has long expressed an interest in Venezuela, which boasts the world’s largest proven crude-oil reserves as of 2023—approximately 303 billion barrels, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).
But the President did not outline how soon, exactly, Americans can expect to feel relief at the pumps. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment on the expected timeline.
The answer is especially relevant amid the ongoing war with Iran. One of the linchpins of the conflict is a Tehran-imposed blockade on the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world’s oil had previously passed. The move has been consequential for the global economy. In the United States, the national average cost for a gallon of gas is $4.08 as of Saturday, according to the AAA, as compared to $3.20 one year ago.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the deal a “huge win” for America in a social media post on Friday, saying that it means “lowering gas prices here at home.”
Any eventual decline in gas prices could provide relief at a time when Americans are already contending with persistent inflation, which was the focus of remarks made by Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh at the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium in Wyoming on Friday.
However, it could be a while before the impact of the new deal with Venezuela is directly felt.
What we know about Trump’s Venezuela oil deal
Much of what is known about the deal comes from a statement released on Telegram by acting Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez late Friday.
“It provides for the development of 17 strategic fields, with a proven potential of 65 billion barrels of oil, more than $100 billion in investment and more than $209 billion in tax revenue for the state,” the statement said. “These investments will contribute not only to the recovery and modernization of our industry, but also to our country’s economic growth, the energy security of our hemisphere and greater stability in international markets.”
Despite its vast oil reserves, the country only produced about 1.1 million barrels per day in July, according to a secondary-source estimate from the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries.
The EIA has attributed Venezuela’s long-term production decline largely to “government mismanagement, international sanctions, and the country’s economic crisis,” which contributed to “a lack of investment and maintenance in the energy sector and a deteriorating infrastructure.” The agency found that Venezuela’s total energy production declined by an average of 8.2% annually between 2011 and 2021.
“The U.S. deal with Venezuela is very important strategically,” says Claudio Galimberti, the chief economist at Rystad Energy. “The new wave of investments that is about to come to Venezuela as a result of this deal will be crucial to turn around the country's aging oil infrastructure. Venezuela will be able to increase its production at a faster rate and unlock barrels that would otherwise have stayed underground.”
The agreement envisions private operators playing a central role in that effort. Rodríguez’s post explained that the agreement allows Venezuela to increase its oil production “through the participation of private operators,” without further elaboration.
A State Department official tells TIME that Rodríguez has granted a private company, which is “a joint project of the U.S. government and an experienced private operator in Venezuela,” 100-year rights to develop the fields, adding: “This new entity will be the second largest corporate holder of proven reserves after Saudi Aramco.”
The deal would give the U.S. 55% of the new company’s effective output, “split between equity ownership and guaranteed at-cost off-take,” the official says.
Although they declined to comment on the expected timeline for these steps, the official adds: "As the company scales production, the resulting stable supply of at-cost oil in our Hemisphere will go toward filling the U.S. strategic petroleum reserve and fulfilling the supply needs of our Great U.S. Military.”
Other key factors also remain unknown—including how the deal will be financed and whether it includes any target dates for achieving various outcomes.
Why gas prices won’t lower immediately
One of the main reasons that Americans are unlikely to see immediate relief from high gas prices is that the deal is linked to 17 oil fields in Venezuela, not access to 65 billion barrels of already-produced crude oil.
While those fields contain proven reserves, Venezuela does not have the infrastructure in place currently to produce the oil at a rate that would significantly and rapidly affect the wallets of everyday Americans.
Such concerns arose after former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro was ousted by the United States in January, when oil executives and analysts assessed the viability of developing the country’s reserves.
Speaking at the White House on Jan. 9, ExxonMobil Chairman and CEO Darren Woods called it “uninvestable,” given his assessment of the “legal and commercial constructs—frameworks—in place today in Venezuela.”
“There's an opportunity in Venezuela with all the resources there,” he said. “We don't have that challenge of finding; we have the challenge of developing those resources.”
Patrick De Haan, the head of petroleum analysis for GasBuddy/PDI, provides a similar assessment. He tells TIME, “While the hope of lower gas prices sounds promising, it still will take billions of investment to get that oil.”
In her statement, Rodríguez said the initiative is expected to “facilitate a significant flow of investment aimed at the recovery and reconstruction of strategic infrastructure for the development of our hydrocarbons industry.”
But it remains unclear where that investment will come from, including whether the private operator will provide the financing and how the project will proceed “at no cost to the American Taxpayer,” as Trump said.
De Haan also questioned whether the agreement’s unusual structure could discourage investment. “How can the U.S. lay claim to a sovereign country’s natural resources?” he says, adding that even with approval from Venezuela’s acting president, a 100-year contract could face legal challenges or prove difficult to enforce.
“That may slow down oil companies from wanting to invest in Venezuela,” he explains.
And financing is only one hurdle; the physical work required also shapes the timeline.
“Drilling and pumping that oil will take a very long time. Changes to fuel prices won’t happen overnight or even in months,” De Haan says, adding that global refining capacity is currently constrained, further limiting the speed at which additional crude supply could affect the market.
Galimberti says that consumers should expect a long road between the initial investment and the ultimate production and distribution of oil.
“You will need to factor in several quarters and, in quite a few cases, years,” he says. “Therefore, it is a deal whose benefits will be seen mostly in the medium-long term.”
“To lower gasoline and diesel prices in the short term, the most effective way by far is by increasing the flows from the Middle East,” Galimberti says. He points to recent successes in bypassing the Strait of Hormuz, including pipelines and ports being developed across the Gulf.
Even without potential legal hurdles from within Venezuela, executing on the promise of the reserves could take years, which means that Americans may be in for a wait before they see the impact at gas stations across the U.S.

articles.title: Air defense forces shoot down 199 of 224 Russian drones during day

Air defense forces shoot down 199 of 224 Russian drones during day
Ukrinform
    Air defense forces shot down 199 attack drones used by Russian troops to attack Ukraine beginning on the morning of August 29.

articles.title: 'Strikes not just near LoC': Ex-Army chief Naravane details how India changed tactics in Op Sindoor
articles.body:
'Strikes not just near LoC': Ex-Army chief Naravane details how India changed tactics in Op Sindoor
Edited by: Kanchan Yadav / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 29, 2026, 18:10 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
May 10, 2025: Screengrab from a video of Army and security personnel during Operation Sindoor (Photo: @adgpi on X via PTI)
NEW DELHI: Former Army chief General M M Naravane on Saturday described Operation Sindoor as "very necessary action", stating that it marked a significant shift in India's approach towards Pakistan. Naravane said India moved beyond targeting terrorist bases along the border to striking their supporters and infrastructure deep inside Pakistan, signalling a more assertive response to cross-border terrorism.Speaking to reporters in Vadodara after attending an event, Naravane, the 28th Chief of the Army Staff, said India’s earlier responses to terror attacks, including the Uri and Pulwama attacks, had largely focused on terrorist hideouts close to the border.
“Operation Sindoor, which took place after the Pahalgam attack, was a very necessary action... Previously, whenever such attacks occurred, like after Uri, and Balakot strikes after Pulwama -- we were mostly targeting terrorist hideouts close to the border,” he said, news agency PTI reported.“But this time, the strikes carried out targeted their supporters and those who provide them backing, wherever they may be -- not just near the Line of Control, but deep inside Pakistan, in Muridke and Bahawalpur, from where they receive this support,” he added.
Naravane said the operation sent a message that those supporting terrorism could not escape Indian action regardless of where they were located.“As our defence minister Rajnath Singh had said, 'we will enter their territory and eliminate them', and there will be no protection for them. So, this was a very significant shift in our modus operandi,” he said.
Naravane dismisses Pak’s ability to take on India
Asked about reports of increased Pakistani activity in the Sir Creek sector and the reported “Operation Ababil”, Naravane said such activities take place but he did not have complete information about the reported operation.“These kinds of activities keep happening. I don't have complete information about this right now since I am retired,” he said.“I would like to say that whatever activity takes place, our forces always keep a close watch on it. There is nothing to panic about, and whatever action needs to be taken, appropriate action will be taken at the right time,” he added.Asked whether Pakistan was capable of taking on India, Naravane replied, “In my opinion, no.”
On India-China border talks
On India-China relations, Naravane said the recent meeting between National Security Advisor Ajit Doval and Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi should be viewed against the backdrop of the long-standing boundary dispute between the two countries.“This discussion that took place, the 25th round of Special Representative-level talks between Ajit Doval from our side and Foreign Minister Wang Yi from China, is not happening for the first time,” he said.Naravane said the lack of a clearly demarcated boundary, both on maps and on the ground, was the key issue behind periodic disputes between the two countries.“Exactly where the boundary lies has not been clearly demarcated either on maps or on the ground. It is because of this lack of demarcation that occasional disputes arise between India and China,” he said.On theatre commands, Naravane said the debate over reorganising the armed forces along integrated theatre lines had been underway since the Kargil War.“The discussion on theaterisation first began after the Kargil War. It has already been 25 to 26 years since then. Theaterisation is not a new concept; it is a continuous process and an evolution,” he said.“Considering the way the nature of modern warfare is transforming and decision cycles are becoming progressively shorter, it is essential that we move toward theaterisation as expeditiously as possible,” the former Army chief added.
Operation Sindoor was a significant demonstration of India's military and strategic capabilities, combining military and non-military measures to neutralise terrorist threats and deter Pakistani aggression. The multi-dimensional operation reinforced India’s zero-tolerance approach to terrorism while maintaining strategic restraint and securing international support.
Kanchan Yadav is a writer at The Times of India, where she covers business, politics, international affairs and social issues. Her reporting also focuses on policy, governance and economic developments, with a close lens on how decisions in corridors of power affect everyday lives and community well-being.

articles.title: Russia launches third attack on Ukraine’s largest Danube port this month, during peak of wheat harvest
articles.body:
A Russian strike on southern Odesa Oblast killed one person overnight and set grain trucks on fire. Five trucks loaded with grain were destroyed and three more damaged, with one person killed and three injured, the head of the Odesa Regional Military Administration, Oleh Kiper, said.
The strike hit the Izmail district, home to Ukraine's largest Danube port. The port became a maritime lifeline after Russia's 2022 Black Sea blockade, carrying the overflow whenever the sea lanes are constrained, National Security Journal reported. The attack is part of a campaign against the food supply.
Ukraine is one of the world's largest suppliers of wheat, maize, and sunflower, so the strikes register far beyond its borders, in the import-dependent countries that buy its grain.
Fire destroyed eight trucks
The attack set eight cargo trucks and dry grass nearby alight, the press service of the State Emergency Service in Odesa Oblast reported. Rescuers have since put out the fires.
"Unfortunately, a person was killed in the attack, and three more were injured," the service said.
The strike hit transport infrastructure
Russia struck the Izmail district overnight on 29 August, damaging transport infrastructure, the Izmail District State Administration reported. The district sits on the Danube close to the Romanian border.
"There are casualties. Sadly, a person has been killed. The injured have been given the necessary help. Representatives of the security structures and medical workers are working at the scene," the administration said.
The Danube corridor is a standing target
The strike fits a pattern. Russia hit Izmail's port infrastructure on 13 August, cutting power in parts of the city, and struck it again days later, damaging a Togo-flagged civilian vessel. The attacks come during Ukraine's peak wheat harvest, expected at around 60 million metric tons this year, close to the 2025 crop. Farmers need the export revenue now to finance next year's sowing, and storage is filling as grain goes unshipped.
Russia's Defense Ministry has described its Izmail strikes as hitting berthing terminals for military cargo and depots for Western-supplied weapons. The trucks burned in this strike were carrying grain.

articles.title: 'Orcas hunt these bears' — Putin says children should learn the 'food chain' to understand Russia's war
articles.body:
'Orcas hunt these bears' — Putin says children should learn the 'food chain' to understand Russia's war
Russian President Vladimir Putin invoked orcas "tearing polar bears apart" as a new analogy for Russia's war against Ukraine while speaking to students and teachers at a Moscow university on Aug. 29, according to the Russian independent media outlet Meduza.
Putin's remarks came as near-continuous air raid alerts across Ukraine stretched into a third consecutive day, with Russia launching continued waves of attacks. The attacks killed at least 37 people in Kyiv Oblast on Aug. 28 and killed a 14-year-old girl and a 2-year-old girl in separate attacks on Aug. 29.
The exchange began when Putin asked a teacher from Russia's Belgorod region, who had visited the North Pole, whether he had seen polar bears there.
After the teacher said he had seen two "enormous" bears, Putin replied that orcas live nearby and eat those bears.
"Right nearby, orcas hunt these bears, devouring them as if they were nothing. They descend in packs — and then, boom, tear them (bears) apart," he said.
Putin then connected the example to Russia's war in Ukraine.
"Yes, that's the food chain. Children should be taught about this, so that they understand what kind of world we live in and why we are conducting the special military operation," Putin said.
The bear is a recurring metaphor in Putin's rhetoric about Russia's confrontation with the West.
In 2014, after Russia had illegally annexed Crimea, he compared Russia to a bear that the West was trying to put "on a chain," warning that its "teeth and claws" would be torn out.
"Maybe our bear should sit quietly, not chasing any piglets around, but just eating honey and berries. Maybe they should just leave him alone? They will not. They are trying to put it on a chain," Putin claimed.

Kyiv • UNN

The British Royal Navy spent three days monitoring Russian ships sailing through British waters. This was reported by UNN, citing The Guardian.

Together with our allies, this approach forces Moscow to divert Russian warships from their primary mission. This is because Russia knows that we are ready to take action again if necessary
Additionally
The Royal Navy recently warned of increased Russian activity in UK waters. In July, it spent 21 days monitoring vessels from Moscow, 25% more than the previous year. Officials say they have repeatedly recorded the presence of warships in the Strait of Dover and the North Sea.
And while Western officials have sought to downplay the likelihood of a direct conflict between Russia and NATO, the Kremlin accused the United Kingdom and its allies of "playing with fire" over their continued support for Ukraine.
Recall
At the beginning of August, the United Kingdom tightened sanctions against Russia: 19 new entities were placed under restrictions. These included banks, companies and the "shadow fleet".

articles.title: What does Ukraine’s new defense minister wear on his wrist? He did not mention it until reporter asked
articles.body:
Ukraine's new defense minister wears his war on his wrist. Yevhenii Khmara's bracelet carries, on each of its chains, the engraved name of a comrade who did not come back from the war, The National Interest reported.
Khmara took over the Defense Ministry on 19 August, replacing Mykhailo Fedorov, whose July dismissal set off nationwide protests. He came to the job from the SBU, Ukraine's Security Service, which he had led for seven months when Ukraine's campaign against Russian oil refining reached its widest scale.
He did not volunteer the story
Khmara did not explain the bracelet until a reporter asked him about it over dinner in Kyiv this month. The names now travel with him into the meetings where decisions about Ukraine's defense are made.
He ran the SBU during the oil campaign
Alpha, the SBU's special operations unit, is a tiny share of Ukraine's armed forces, yet the service's own accounting credits it with an outsized share of the damage inflicted on Russia, up to 20 percent of all enemy infantry losses.
More telling is what happened to Russian oil during his seven months in charge of the service. Ukraine's General Staff now estimates that nearly 43 percent of Russia's refining capacity has been knocked out. To a large extent, this is the result of the campaign Khmara helped oversee.
Khmara also developed a doctrine of ruthless cost asymmetry: strike operations designed to cost roughly 2 percent of the economic damage they inflict, targeting not individual facilities but critical nodes within the system.
Khmara insisted that part of the staff of the previous minister stayed
Earlier, Khmara has proposed that the core of the former Defense Ministry team remain in their positions. In particular, this concerns specialists responsible for procurement reform.
Mstyslav Banik, who served as a deputy to Fedorov, confirmed that he was staying on under the newly appointed defense minister. He led a central part of the ministry's modernization and is responsible for implementing the defense procurement reform.

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf on Saturday rejected US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s claims that Washington’s blockade and economic measures would crush the Iranian economy.

Tensions between Tehran and Washington have remained high since the war began with strikes on Iran in late February. Iran retaliated by targeting US military positions and assets in Arab countries aligned with Washington.
